caption: The field around the evolved star IRS 3 near the Milky Way's centre, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Countless stars crowd this frame, set against glowing clouds of red, orange, pink, white and blue. A bright, almost white concentration of stars sits at the centre, wrapped in fine filaments of lit-up gas and dust, while dark, opaque patches of dust cut into the glow, especially on the left. This is the neighbourhood of IRS 3, a highly evolved star lying only 0.55 light-years from Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the heart of our galaxy.

Webb combined its near-infrared and mid-infrared cameras to produce what the team describes as the most detailed mid-infrared view yet of this field. That matters because this whole region is bathed in intense radiation from the surroundings of the black hole.

Even so, an international team found that dust and even water can form and survive surprisingly close to Sagittarius A*. IRS 3 keeps seeding its surroundings with freshly made material despite the harsh environment.
explore: The Galactic Centre lies about 26,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. The picture draws on four separate Webb observing programmes led by J. Lu, F. Yusef-Zadeh, N. B. Sabha and C. Chan, whose data were combined into this single view.

understand.summary: This view combines Webb's NIRCam (near-infrared) and MIRI (mid-infrared) instruments across nine filters. Shorter wavelengths are shown in purple, blue and cyan, and progressively longer ones in green, yellow, orange and red; some filters trace molecular hydrogen, hydrogen emission, carbon-rich PAH molecules and silicate dust.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye, so every colour here is assigned to make the data readable.

alt: A dense star field over glowing red, orange, pink, white and blue clouds, with a bright white core of stars at the centre, wispy filaments radiating outward, and dark dust patches toward the left.

caption: The star-forming region N90 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright blue stars, freshly formed, sit inside a hollow they have carved in the middle of a nebula. Around them, the cloud's outer reaches remain, and beyond those a scattering of distant galaxies shows through, tinted reddish-brown by dust. This is N90, a star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way.

The young stars are hot, and they pour out high-energy radiation. That radiation is wearing the nebula away from the inside. The thin outer parts of the cloud stop the energetic outflows from escaping straight out of the cluster, so the erosion works on the nebula's edges from within.

N90 sits well away from the main body of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Because of that position, many far more distant galaxies can be seen in Hubble's view. They form a grand backdrop for the stellar newcomers, and dust in the region gives them a reddish-brown tint.
explore: The region, also catalogued with the star cluster NGC 602, is listed at a distance of about 200,000 light-years, in the direction of the constellation Hydrus. The image comes from the Hubble Heritage Team working with the ESA/Hubble collaboration.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this scene through visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter captures light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's long exposures reveal faint background galaxies far beyond what any eye could detect.

alt: Bright blue young stars inside a cavity in a nebula, with many small reddish-brown background galaxies visible around it.

caption: The bulge fossil fragment Terzan 5, imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
story: Thousands of tiny white, orange and blue points pack this frame like a shaken snow globe. They crowd into a roughly round swarm at the centre and thin out toward the edges, where a few larger orange stars carry prominent diffraction spikes. This is Terzan 5, a stellar system orbiting inside the bulge of the Milky Way, the bright, crowded central region of our galaxy that is also thick with gas and dust.

Terzan 5 was long classified as a globular cluster. Astronomers already knew it held two groups of stars of very different ages. Combining Webb and Hubble data, a team found strong evidence for two more, dating from 3.8 billion and just 2.5 billion years ago, and pinned the older groups at 12.5 billion and 4.7 billion years.

That mix proved Terzan 5 is not a globular cluster at all. It belongs to a new category, the bulge fossil fragment: a self-contained system that enriches itself, building generations of stars with different ages and iron content.
explore: Terzan 5 lies about 22,000 light-years away in Sagittarius. Its mass, about 2 million times the Sun's, is squeezed into a system just a few tens of light-years wide, which makes it one of the most massive and densely packed cluster-like systems in the Milky Way.

understand.summary: This combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light (shown in blue and cyan) with Webb's NIRCam in infrared light (shown in orange and red).
understand.eye: The Webb data are infrared and invisible to the eye, which helps see through the dust that fills the galaxy's bulge.

scaleExtra: Terzan 5 is 22,000 light-years away, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: A dense field of thousands of white, orange and blue stars concentrated in a roughly circular swarm at the centre, with larger orange stars showing diffraction spikes near the edges.

caption: The star cluster NGC 346 and star-forming region N66, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A brilliant cluster of stars sits at the centre of this view, ringed by arched, ragged filaments with a distinct ridge. The dark edge of that ridge, seen in silhouette, is beaded with fine detail. This is NGC 346, the cluster at the heart of the star-forming region N66 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

The region is one of the most active and intricately structured places where stars are being born. Hot stars in the cluster give off a torrent of radiation that eats into the denser gas around them, carving the dust and gas into sculpted shapes.

Look along the ridge and you can find several small globules of dust. Each one points back toward the central cluster, like a windsock caught in a strong wind. That alignment suggests they are being shaped by the radiation streaming outward from the young stars at the centre.
explore: The region lies about 210,000 light-years away, far beyond our own galaxy, in the direction of the constellation Tucana. Hubble's view shows how the radiation from a young cluster can reshape the cloud in which its stars were born.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this view through visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the long exposures reveal fine dusty detail no eye could pick out at this distance.

alt: A bright star cluster at the centre surrounded by arched, ragged filaments of gas and a dark, beaded ridge of dust seen in silhouette.
flags: distance conflict: packet says 170000 light years, caption says 210,000

caption: NGC 2264 with the Christmas Tree cluster and the Cone Nebula, imaged by ESO's La Silla Observatory
story: Sparkling blue stars stand out in this colour view of NGC 2264, a patch of sky containing the Christmas Tree star cluster as well as the Cone Nebula. The Christmas Tree is a star cluster, while the Cone Nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in the same region.

The picture was built from four separate exposures, each through a different filter: blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha. Combining them lets astronomers show both the light of the stars and the glow of hydrogen gas in one frame. The camera that took them is the Wide Field Imager, which sits on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory.

La Silla stands 2400 metres high, in Chile's Atacama Desert among the Andean foothills. Wide-field cameras like this one are well suited to sweeping regions of sky that are too large for narrower instruments.
explore: The region shown here is about 30 light-years across. NGC 2264 is listed at a distance of about 3000 light-years, in the constellation Monoceros.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, made with B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so the faint glowing gas looks far brighter here than it would to the eye.

alt: A colour view of the NGC 2264 region with sparkling blue stars of the Christmas Tree cluster and the Cone Nebula.

caption: Herbig-Haro 49/50 and a background spiral galaxy, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A cone-shaped, orange-red cloud angles from the upper left toward the lower right, its upper end rounded and translucent. Right at that tip sits a spiral galaxy with a blue centre fading into red arms. The cloud is Herbig-Haro 49/50, an outflow from a nearby star that is still forming within the Milky Way. The galaxy is a chance alignment, far more distant.

Young protostars generally launch narrow jets of material. As this jet races outward, it slams into the surrounding dust and gas, like the wake behind a speeding boat, and piles it into arcs. That material is squeezed and heated, then cools by giving off light, and Webb's infrared view picks out molecular hydrogen and carbon monoxide within it.

The background galaxy has a prominent blue central bulge of older stars and hints of side lobes, suggesting it could be a barred spiral. Reddish clumps in its arms mark warm dust and groups of young stars.
explore: The outflow's intricate features help astronomers understand how young stars form and how their jets affect the space around them. Many more galaxies lie further away in the background, some shining right through the diffuse infrared glow of the Herbig-Haro object. The object lies in the direction of Chamaeleon.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam (near-infrared) and MIRI (mid-infrared) instruments captured this view. Shorter wavelengths are shown in blue and cyan, a middle band in green, a molecular hydrogen filter in orange, and a MIRI filter tracing carbon-rich PAH molecules in red.
understand.eye: This is all infrared light, invisible to the eye; the colours are assigned so the different features can be told apart.

alt: A conical orange-red cloud angled from the upper left to lower right, with a spiral galaxy with a blue centre and red arms at its rounded upper end, against a black background dotted with stars and faint galaxies.

caption: The Eagle Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: The famous Pillars of Creation stand at the centre of this wide view of the Eagle Nebula, also known as Messier 16. Around them, other pillars rise from the same star-forming region, and a huge number of stars are scattered across the frame, some in front of the nebula, some inside it and some behind. In the middle left stands another large column, known as the Spire.

To the upper right is a cluster of bright stars, NGC 6611. Its stars are massive and hot, and it is their light that illuminates the pillars. Pillars like these are dense clouds of gas and dust where new stars can form.

The picture is a mosaic, stitched from several images taken at La Silla Observatory by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide-Field Imager camera. A wide-field view shows the pillars in context, as part of a much larger nebula, rather than in close-up.
explore: The Eagle Nebula is listed at a distance of about 7000 light-years, in the constellation Serpens Cauda. The nebula also carries the catalogue number NGC 6611, the same as its central cluster.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light composite from the Wide-Field Imager, using three filters: B shown in blue, V in green and R in red.
understand.eye: The colours roughly follow the filters' own colours, but long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the faint nebula appears much brighter here than it would through an eyepiece.

alt: A wide view of the Eagle Nebula with the Pillars of Creation at the centre, a bright star cluster at upper right, a tall pillar at middle left, and many stars throughout.

caption: The star cluster NGC 3293, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Young stars huddle together in this view, set against clouds of glowing gas and lanes of dust. This is the star cluster NGC 3293, photographed at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager.

The cluster was not always this bright group of stars. About ten million years ago it would have been only a cloud of gas and dust. As stars began to form inside that cloud, it turned into the cluster seen here. In astronomical terms, that makes these stars youthful.

Clusters like NGC 3293 act as natural laboratories. Because their stars formed together from the same cloud at around the same time, they share a common starting point, which lets astronomers compare how stars of different masses change as they age. Studying them helps build a picture of how stars evolve over their lives.
explore: NGC 3293 is listed at a distance of about 8000 light-years, in the direction of the southern constellation Carina.

understand.summary: This view comes from the Wide Field Imager, using B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters that span visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the long exposures bring out faint glowing gas that would be invisible through an eyepiece.

alt: A group of young stars clustered together in front of clouds of glowing gas crossed by lanes of dust.

caption: The actively forming star system Lynds 483, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A thin, vertical cloud shaped roughly like an hourglass runs through the centre of this image, its edges ragged. The top lobe is shown in full, fading away at the top, while the lower lobe is slightly cut off. This is Lynds 483, or L483, and its lobes are shimmering material thrown out by two stars that are still forming.
Young stars often eject material as they grow, and that material slams into the gas and dust around them. Webb's sharp near-infrared view brings out new detail and structure inside these lobes.

Among the most intriguing features are asymmetrical lines that seem to run into one another. The high resolution of Webb's camera is what makes such fine structure visible at all, revealing detail inside the lobes that had not been seen before. The light it records is near-infrared, beyond the red end of what our eyes can detect.
explore: L483 lies about 650 light-years away, in the constellation Serpens. The image was taken with Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, NIRCam.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. The two shortest-wavelength filters are shown in blue, a filter tracing carbon-rich PAH molecules in cyan, another in yellow, and a molecular hydrogen filter in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours are assigned to separate the different kinds of emission.

alt: A thin vertical hourglass-shaped cloud with irregular edges at the centre, its top lobe fading out at the top and its lower lobe slightly cut off.

caption: The giant star AG Carinae and its nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An expanding shell of gas and dust surrounds a single brilliant star in this Hubble portrait. The star is AG Carinae, one of the brightest stars that can be seen in our galaxy, and the picture was made to mark the 31st anniversary of Hubble's launch.

AG Carinae is a giant, and it lives in a precarious balance. Its own gravity pulls inward while the intense radiation it produces pushes outward. The star is locked in this tug-of-war to avoid tearing itself apart.

The shell around it is expanding outward into space and is about five light-years wide. That is the same as the distance from the Sun to Alpha Centauri, our nearest neighbouring star system. Hubble's sharp view lets astronomers study the structure of such shells in detail.
explore: AG Carinae is listed at a distance of about 15,000 light-years, in the constellation Carina. Hubble captured it with its Wide Field Camera 3, using filters that include ultraviolet light.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet part of the data is invisible to the human eye, and the long exposures reveal a faint shell that the eye could not pick out.

alt: A bright star at the centre of an expanding shell of gas and dust.

caption: A giant stellar jet in the proto-cluster Sh2-284, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Yellow-orange filaments bunch together just above the centre, looking like a rose seen from the side. From that knot, two red lobes stretch toward the upper left and lower right, each a tall, narrow triangle with a rounded tip, built from wavy, irregular lines. A bright white star with eight diffraction spikes sits at the top of the rose.

The red lobes belong to an extremely large stellar jet, a Herbig-Haro object: streams of plasma blasting out from newly formed stars. Webb found it in Sh2-284, a proto-cluster on the outskirts of the Milky Way, where a group of stars is still in the making.

Its size is what makes it important. Its detection provides evidence that such jets scale with the mass of the stars powering them: the heavier the star driving the plasma, the bigger the jet it produces.
explore: Dozens of other stars are scattered across the field, including a bright blue star with especially prominent diffraction spikes to the lower left of the rose. The proto-cluster lies in the direction of the constellation Monoceros.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. The shorter-wavelength filters are shown in blue and green, and the longest ones, which trace hydrogen emission and molecular hydrogen, in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours are chosen to separate glowing gas from starlight.

scaleExtra: The jet is 8 light-years across, about double the distance from the Sun to the Alpha Centauri system, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: Yellow-orange filaments shaped like a side-on rose above centre, with long red triangular lobes of wavy lines extending to the upper left and lower right, and bright stars with diffraction spikes on a black background.

caption: The Butterfly Star, IRAS 04302+2247, imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
story: A dense, dark streak of dusty gas runs vertically through this view, with two gauzy clouds spreading out on either side. The streak is a planet-forming disc seen edge-on around the young star IRAS 04302+2247, which lies in a dark cloud in the Taurus star-forming region. The dust blocks the star's bright light, and the two clouds, lit by reflected starlight, have earned it the nickname the Butterfly Star.

The star is a protostar, still gathering mass from its surroundings. Webb measures its disc at 65 billion kilometres across, several times the width of our Solar System. The disc's gas and dust is raw material in which young planets could grow.

Seen face-on, such discs can show rings, gaps and spirals. Edge-on, this one reveals its vertical structure instead. Dust grains sink toward the disc's midplane into a thin, dense layer that favours planet formation, so the disc's thickness shows how efficiently that settling has worked.
explore: Discs like this can help researchers understand what happened roughly 4.5 billion years ago, when the Sun and planets formed. Hubble's data highlight clumps and streaks around the dust lane that suggest the star is still feeding and launching jets and outflows. The system lies about 525 light-years away.

understand.summary: This combines Hubble's WFPC2 camera in optical light (shown in blue) with Webb's NIRCam and MIRI in infrared light, with longer wavelengths shown progressively in blue, cyan, green, orange and red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the reflected glow would be far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A narrow dark vertical band of dusty gas with two gauzy, glowing clouds spreading out on either side of it.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 604 in the Triangulum Galaxy, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Clumpy red clouds with filament-like strands fill the centre of this frame. On their centre-right is a large, cavernous bubble holding a hazy blue glow sprinkled with stars, its rim edged in white dust, and smaller bubbles sit near the top. This is NGC 604, a star-forming region in the Triangulum Galaxy, a neighbouring galaxy also known as M33.

The hollows are the work of bright, hot young stars, whose winds blow cavities in the surrounding gas and dust. Webb's infrared camera sorts that material by type. Bright orange streaks mark carbon-based molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs.

Farther from the cavities, deeper red traces molecular hydrogen, cooler gas that is a prime place for new stars to form. Hydrogen that has been ionised by ultraviolet radiation shows up as the ghostly white and blue glow. Together they map how young stars reshape the cloud that made them.
explore: NGC 604 lies 2.73 million light-years from Earth. It offers astronomers a nearby place to examine a dense concentration of very young, massive stars. A few disc-shaped background galaxies and some small red stars are scattered around the image.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with the shortest filters shown in blue and cyan, a middle band in green, a PAH filter in yellow and the longest filters, including molecular hydrogen, in red.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye; the colours are assigned to separate the different kinds of gas and dust.

alt: Clumpy red filamentary clouds on black, with a large bubble at centre-right containing a blue glow with stars and white dust at its edges, and smaller bubbles near the top.

caption: The Sagittarius B2 molecular cloud, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A wide field of stars, broken up by clumps of orange cloud, fills this view. It shows Sagittarius B2, a molecular cloud near the centre of our galaxy, as seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera. A molecular cloud is a cold, dense region of gas and dust, the kind of place where new stars can form.

In near-infrared light, stars, gas and dust in the cloud all glow. This particular kind of light shows more of the region's diverse, colourful stars, but less of the structure in its gas and dust than other views do.

That trade-off is why astronomers use more than one instrument. Each of Webb's instruments adds its own piece of information, and together they help build a fuller picture of what is going on in this part of the galactic centre. This near-infrared image is one part of that larger set of observations.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam using eleven filters. The shortest wavelengths are shown in blue, then cyan, green, yellow and orange, with the longest, including a carbon monoxide filter, in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours are assigned to reveal differences between stars and clouds.

alt: A wide region of space filled with stars and clumps of orange clouds.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 10, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view looks into the brightest part of the core of Messier 10, a globular cluster, which is a dense ball of stars. The region shown is about 13 light-years across.

Messier 10 owes its catalogue name to Charles Messier, the 18th-century French astronomer who mainly hunted comets. Through the telescopes of his day, comets, nebulae, star clusters and galaxies all looked like faint, fuzzy blobs. The difference was motion: comets drift slowly against the background stars, while the others stay put. Messier listed the fixed objects so they would not be mistaken for comets, and his list of just over 100 entries now includes many of the sky's best-known sights. Messier 10 appeared in the very first edition, published in 1774, which had 45 objects.

The cluster is roughly 80 light-years across, so in principle it should look about two thirds the size of the Moon. Yet its outskirts are extremely diffuse, and even its brighter core is too faint for the unaided eye.
explore: Messier 10 lies about 15 000 light-years away in Ophiuchus. The observations came from a large Hubble survey of the Milky Way's globular clusters. A contestant called flashenthunder entered a version of the image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition, which invited enthusiasts to search the archive.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The cluster's core is too dim to see with the naked eye, and the near-infrared data are invisible to it; Hubble's long exposures reveal its individual stars.

alt: A dense field of stars from the bright core of a globular cluster.

caption: The young star cluster NGC 1333 in Perseus, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Soft, wispy clouds of gas and dust spread across this mosaic, with thin, finely layered structures pressed together at the centre. Large, bright stars carry six long spikes of light, and smaller stars lie buried in the clouds. Near the stars the clouds glow blue, while orange marks gas shining in infrared light. This is NGC 1333, a young star-forming cluster in the Perseus molecular cloud.
Those orange patches are Herbig-Haro objects, which form when ionised material thrown out by young stars crashes into the surrounding cloud. They are signs of a very busy star-forming site.

Webb's sensitivity lets astronomers probe objects of extremely low mass. Some of the faintest 'stars' here are actually newborn free-floating brown dwarfs, with masses comparable to giant planets. On the right, the shadow of an edge-on disc around a young star appears as two dark cones against a bright background.
explore: Hubble featured this cluster as its 33rd anniversary image, but dust hid much of the action. The cluster is only 1–3 million years old and about 960 light-years away. Our Sun formed 4.6 billion years ago in a similar dusty cloud, as part of a cluster perhaps even more massive than this one.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from Webb's NIRISS instrument in near-infrared light, with the shorter-wavelength filter shown in blue and green and the longer one in green and red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust that hid much of this cluster in Hubble's earlier view.

alt: Wispy clouds of gas and dust with finely layered structures at the centre, bright six-pointed stars scattered throughout, blue glow near stars and orange glowing patches.

caption: The super star cluster Westerlund 1, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A dense crowd of bright stars fills this frame, each carrying six large and two small diffraction spikes from the telescope's optics. Their sizes and colours vary with brightness, distance and type, and patches of billowing red gas glow around them. This is Westerlund 1, an open cluster that sits behind a vast interstellar cloud of dust and gas.

It is a super star cluster, holding hundreds of very massive stars packed together. Its population has no match elsewhere in the Milky Way, spanning Wolf-Rayet stars, OB supergiants, yellow hypergiants and luminous blue variables. Some shine with almost a million times the Sun's brilliance. Because such stars live short lives, the cluster must be very young, estimated at between 3.5 and 5 million years old.
Super star clusters are thought to be where most of our galaxy's stars formed long ago. Only a few remain, so Westerlund 1 offers a rare window on that era.
explore: The cluster lies roughly 12 000 light-years away in Ara and was discovered in 1961 by Bengt Westerlund. Astronomers believe it holds between 50 000 and 100 000 times the Sun's mass in a region less than six light-years across. Within 40 million years it may host more than 1 500 supernovae.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam taken for the EWOCS survey, with the shorter-wavelength filters shown in blue, middle ones in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it lets Webb see through the dust cloud that dims this cluster in visible light.

alt: A dense cluster of bright stars of varied sizes and colours with eight-pointed diffraction spikes, surrounded by patches of billowing red gas against distant stars and galaxies on black.

caption: The central part of the star cluster IC 348, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Fine, hair-like pink-purple filaments fill the middle of this image, curving to either side of the centre. On the right they form a dramatic loop that seems to reach toward the viewer, while yellowish filaments sit at lower left. Two bright stars near the centre show Webb's eight-point spikes. This is the heart of IC 348, a star cluster.

The wispy curtains are a reflection nebula, interstellar material bouncing back the light of the cluster's stars. It also contains carbon-bearing molecules called PAHs. The bright star closest to the centre is really a pair of type B stars, the most massive in the cluster, and their winds may help shape the large loop.

Astronomers searched IC 348 for free-floating brown dwarfs: bodies with too little mass to be stars, yet bigger than most planets. They found three with less than eight times Jupiter's mass. The smallest weighs only three to four times as much as Jupiter, which challenges theories of how stars form.
explore: IC 348 is listed at a distance of about 1000 light-years, in the constellation Perseus.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam using three filters, with the shortest wavelength shown in blue, the middle in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint brown dwarfs would be far too dim to see without a large telescope.

alt: Pink-purple hair-like filaments curving across the middle, forming a loop on the right, with yellowish filaments at lower left and two bright stars with eight-point spikes near the centre.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 69, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of white, silvery stars crowd this view, with a few foreground stars standing out large and golden against them. This is the globular cluster Messier 69, or M 69, a dense collection of old stars.

M 69 stands out for its chemistry. As globular clusters go, it is one of the most metal-rich known. In astronomy, a 'metal' is any element heavier than hydrogen and helium, the two most common elements in the Universe. Every one of those heavier elements, from the calcium in bones to the carbon in diamonds, was forged by nuclear fusion in stars, and each generation of stars has added to the supply.

Globular cluster stars are ancient, so their metal content is much lower than that of younger stars such as the Sun. Measuring what these old stars are made of has helped astronomers trace how the cosmos has changed over time.
explore: M 69 lies 29 700 light-years away in Sagittarius, the Archer. The famed comet hunter Charles Messier added it to his catalogue, and it also carries an NGC catalogue number. The image covers a field of about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This view combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates thousands of individual stars.

alt: Thousands of white, silvery stars packed together, with a few larger golden foreground stars.

caption: The young open cluster IC 1590 in the Pacman Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The brightest stars at the core of the young open cluster IC 1590 appear toward the top of this view, and a dark region below is part of the hungry mouth of the Pacman Nebula, NGC 281. The star-forming region takes its nickname from its resemblance to the arcade game character.

Pacman is not really eating these stars. Instead, its gas and dust are raw material for making new ones. The cluster's stars are, in a sense, planning their escape: open clusters are only loosely held together, and this group is expected to drift apart within a few tens of millions of years.

Through small telescopes, the core of the cluster looks like a triple star, while the surrounding nebula is much fainter and very hard to spot. The American astronomer E. E. Barnard first recorded the nebula in the late nineteenth century, using a 15 cm telescope.
explore: IC 1590 lies about ten thousand light-years away in Cassiopeia. The total exposure times were 450, 1017 and 678 seconds for the three filters, and the frame spans about 3.3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A yellow filter is shown in blue and an orange filter in green; a red filter isolating glowing hydrogen completes the set, with its display colour not specified.
understand.eye: The nebula is very hard to see through small telescopes, but Hubble's long exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

alt: Bright young stars at the top of the frame above a dark region of nebula.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6642, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view looks into the core of NGC 6642, a globular cluster in our own galaxy whose centre is packed so tightly with stars that it is a hard target for most telescopes. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of stars held together by gravity.

That crowding cuts both ways. Because the stars in such a cluster share a similar age, together they preserve clues to the chemical makeup of the Milky Way early in its history. Yet the same density makes individual stars near the core hard to pick apart. NGC 6642 adds a further problem: it sits in a very central part of our galaxy, so any picture of it also catches many 'field stars' that are not part of the cluster at all.

Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys can identify and remove those interlopers and resolve the crowded core in unprecedented detail. Studies with it have turned up many 'blue stragglers', stars that seem to age more slowly than their neighbours, and shown that the cluster is short of low-mass stars.
explore: The cluster lies about 25,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius. The picture combines visible and infrared exposures from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel and covers a patch of sky roughly 1.6 arcminutes on each side.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars in a core that most telescopes cannot resolve.

alt: A crowded field of stars thickening toward the dense core of the globular cluster NGC 6642.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 1805 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars of many colours crowd together in this Hubble image, some blue and others red. This is NGC 1805, a tight globular cluster of thousands of stars close to the rim of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy that orbits the Milky Way.

The stars here swarm around one another like bees around a hive. In the dense centre of such a cluster, stars sit 100 to 1000 times closer together than the Sun's nearest stellar neighbours are to us, so crowded that planetary systems around them are considered unlikely.

The contrast in colour comes from combining two kinds of light: the blue stars are brightest in near-ultraviolet light, the red ones in red and near-infrared light. Hubble can record ultraviolet because it sits above Earth's atmosphere, which absorbs most of it. NGC 1805 is unusual in another way too. Rather than a single generation, it appears to host two populations of stars whose ages differ by millions of years.
explore: Visible from the southern hemisphere, this young globular cluster lies in the constellation Dorado, whose name is Portuguese for dolphinfish. Studying clusters like it helps astronomers work out how stars evolve and what decides whether a star ends as a white dwarf or explodes as a supernova.

understand.summary: This picture comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines near-ultraviolet light, in which the blue stars shine brightest, with red and near-infrared light, which brings out the red stars. The exact colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye and mostly absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, so only a telescope above the atmosphere can record it like this.

alt: A tightly packed cluster of many blue and red stars.

caption: The protoplanetary disc around HL Tauri, imaged by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)
story: This is the disc of material surrounding the young star HL Tauri, seen by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in what ESO describes as the sharpest image the observatory had ever taken. Dark patches lie within the disc, and ALMA revealed substructures there that had never been seen before.

A protoplanetary disc is the flattened ring of gas and dust around a newborn star, the raw material from which planets are thought to form. The detail here is sharper than the Hubble Space Telescope routinely achieves in visible light, and that sharpness is what lets such fine structure show up.

Most intriguing of all, the observations may show where planets are taking shape: the dark patches could mark the positions of planets in the process of forming. ALMA works at millimetre wavelengths, picking up a faint glow from the disc that visible-light telescopes cannot see.
explore: HL Tauri lies about 450 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Taurus. ALMA is an array of many antennas that work together as a single telescope, and this view was made at a wavelength of 1.28 millimetres.

understand.summary: ALMA observed this disc in millimetre-wavelength light, at 1.28 mm. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Millimetre-wavelength light is invisible to the eye, so this picture is a rendering of that signal rather than a view anyone could see through an eyepiece.

alt: The disc around the young star HL Tauri, with dark patches within it.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6440, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A round swarm of stars fills this Webb view, with a tight knot of bright white stars at its centre, larger yellow stars scattered across the frame, and many stars showing spiky diffraction patterns against black space. This is NGC 6440, a globular cluster roughly 28,000 light-years away in Sagittarius, first discovered by William Herschel.

Globular clusters are roughly spherical, tightly bound groups of old stars. NGC 6440 is massive and rich in metals, and it formed and still orbits inside the Galactic bulge, the dense, near-spherical crowd of old stars in the Milky Way's inner region.

Webb's near-infrared camera was used to study the cluster's stars and its pulsars, rapidly spinning, strongly magnetised neutron stars whose beams sweep past us as pulses. The data give the first evidence from Webb of varying helium and oxygen abundances among a globular cluster's stars. Heavy crowding and reddening by interstellar dust had put such bulge clusters out of reach of other telescopes.
explore: Globular clusters hold hundreds of thousands to millions of stars, on average about one light-year apart, though they can be packed as tightly as the span of our Solar System. The fastest known pulsars spin more than 716 times per second, and in theory one could reach 1500 before losing energy or breaking apart.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with the shortest-wavelength filter shown in blue, two middle filters in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes more easily through the interstellar dust that reddens and dims this cluster in visible light.

alt: A spherical cluster of stars filling the frame, with bright white stars concentrated at the centre, larger yellow stars scattered around, and diffraction spikes on many stars against a black background.

caption: The star cluster NGC 1866 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars fill this image from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. They belong to NGC 1866, a star cluster on the outermost fringes of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way. The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.

NGC 1866 is a surprisingly young globular cluster, and it is close enough for its stars to be studied one by one. Most globular clusters are dominated by old stars with low metallicity; astronomers call any element other than hydrogen and helium a 'metal'. Because stars forge heavier elements over their lives, a star built from unenriched material is taken to be very old, and some globular cluster stars may be among the first to form after the Big Bang.

Here, though, the stars are not all alike. Different generations are thought to live side by side. One idea is that after its first stars formed, the cluster met a giant gas cloud that triggered a fresh wave of star birth, producing a younger population and explaining its youthful look.
explore: How globular clusters form is still debated. Star clusters like this one are bound together by gravity and can contain hundreds of thousands of stars. James Dunlop, who found NGC 1866, went on to list thousands of stars and deep-sky objects over his career.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using five filters from the U band through visible light to the near-infrared I band. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble separates individual stars in a cluster belonging to another galaxy, something no eye could do, and part of the light it recorded lies beyond what the eye can see.

alt: A field densely filled with the stars of the cluster NGC 1866.

caption: The starburst region NGC 3603, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A star cluster sits amid richly textured clouds of gas and dust in this wide view from ESO's Very Large Telescope. This is NGC 3603, a starburst region: a place where stars are forming at a furious pace from the nebula's sprawling clouds of gas and dust.

About 22,000 light-years from the Sun, NGC 3603 is the closest known region of its kind in our galaxy. That makes it a valuable local test bed. Intense bursts of star formation like this are very common in other galaxies, but those are so far away that the process is hard to study in detail there.

The image was made with the FORS instrument on one of the four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes of the VLT at Cerro Paranal in Chile. It combines exposures through three filters, two in visible light and one in the near-infrared, and shows a wide field around the cluster, bringing out the texture of its surroundings.
explore: The picture spans a field 7 arcminutes wide and was assembled from exposures through the V, R and I filters. NGC 3603 lies in the direction of the constellation Carina, and ESO has also offered this view as a mounted print in its shop.

understand.summary: This is a three-colour composite from the FORS instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using visible (V and R) and near-infrared (I) filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the long exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

alt: A star cluster surrounded by textured clouds of gas and dust.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 3201, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image looks into NGC 3201, a glistening, ancient globular cluster of hundreds of thousands of stars held together by gravity. James Dunlop found it in 1826 and described it as 'pretty large, pretty bright', becoming 'rather irregular' towards its centre.

Globular clusters surround all large galaxies, yet how they formed and what part they played in building galaxies is still unclear. NGC 3201 recently added a twist: astronomers found a black hole at its heart, betrayed by a star being flung quickly around a massive, invisible partner.

The cluster also stands out among the Milky Way's more than 150 globulars. It moves extremely fast relative to the Sun, and its orbit around the galactic centre is retrograde, running against the usual direction. That behaviour hints that it may have come from outside our galaxy and been captured. Yet its stars are chemically very like those of other globulars in the Milky Way, suggesting they formed at a similar place and time.
explore: The cluster lies about 16,000 light-years away in the constellation Vela. Whether it was adopted by the Milky Way or simply evolved differently from the clusters it grew up with remains an open question.

understand.summary: This view combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in ultraviolet and near-ultraviolet light with its Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the black hole at the cluster's heart cannot be seen at all; it was found only through a star's motion.

alt: A dense, glistening gathering of stars in the globular cluster NGC 3201.

caption: Carbon monoxide gas in the debris disc around HD 181327, imaged by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)
story: A ring of gas encircles the star HD 181327 in this view from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), which maps the density of carbon monoxide within the star's disc of debris. HD 181327 is an F-type star, and this is the first time the gas has been detected around a star of that type.

Only molecular hydrogen is more common than carbon monoxide in the space between the stars, but the gas had previously been found only around a few A-type stars, which are considerably more massive and luminous. HD 181327 belongs to the Beta Pictoris moving group and lies almost 170 light-years from Earth.

The gas sits alongside the dust grains in the ring and was produced recently. One possible source is destructive collisions between icy planetesimals, which usually need larger bodies to nudge them into smashing together hard enough. The ice's inferred make-up resembles the comets of our Solar System, hinting that icy comets could be common around Sun-like stars.
explore: Astronomers used 39 of ALMA's 66 antennas, which sit on the Chajnantor plateau high in the Chilean Andes, at an altitude of 5000 metres. The results appeared in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, in a paper by S. Marino and colleagues titled 'Exocometary gas in the HD 181327 debris ring'.

understand.summary: ALMA observed at millimetre wavelengths (around 220 GHz), and this view maps carbon monoxide gas in the disc. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Millimetre-wavelength light is invisible to the eye; this is a map of gas that no visible-light telescope could show.

alt: A ring of gas around the star HD 181327.

caption: The ringed dusty disc around the young star HD 169142, imaged by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)
story: Vivid rings, separated by deep gaps, circle the young star HD 169142 in this image from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The rings are thick bands of dust, and ALMA captured them sharply by detecting weak signals from the disc's millimetre-sized grains.

ALMA is built to study cold gas and dust, and it has revealed many young planetary systems with similar gaps and cavities. Several explanations have been proposed, including turbulence from an effect called magnetorotational instability and dust grains fusing together, but the most plausible is that giant protoplanets carved the gaps.

As a planetary system forms, gas and dust gather into planets, which then sweep their orbits clean and herd the leftover material into sharp bands. The deep gaps here fit the presence of several protoplanets, in agreement with optical and infrared studies of the same star. Watching discs like this lets scientists probe the first steps of planet formation.
explore: HD 169142 is a young, isolated star about 380 light-years away in the direction of Sagittarius. ALMA recorded this disc at a wavelength of about 1.3 millimetres, using its Band 6 receivers.

understand.summary: ALMA imaged the disc in millimetre-wavelength light at 1.3 mm, tracing the glow of dust grains. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: This millimetre light is invisible to the eye; the image shows the glow of cold dust that visible-light telescopes cannot pick up in this way.

alt: A disc around a young star made of rings of dust separated by deep gaps.

caption: The star-forming region RCW 108 in Ara, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Bright and dark nebulae spread across this wide-field view, with the star cluster NGC 6193 on the left. The subject is RCW 108, a molecular cloud that is being destroyed by intense ultraviolet radiation from heavy, hot stars in that neighbouring cluster.

The complex belongs to Ara OB1, a star-forming association deep in the southern sky in the constellation Ara, the Altar. A molecular cloud is a cold, dense cloud of gas and dust where new stars can form; here, radiation from stars that have already formed is eroding that raw material.

The picture was taken with the Wide Field Imager, a camera made from a mosaic of detectors that covers a large patch of sky at once. It combines 12 separate images. Through each filter, four frames were taken with the telescope shifted slightly between them, so that the gaps between the camera's eight detectors were filled in.
explore: Each full frame records over 67 million pixels across a field 32 arcminutes square. Exposures lasted 300 seconds per frame through the hydrogen-alpha filter and 60 seconds in B and V. Very faint seams may show where frames were joined, and star colours are slightly misaligned at the far corners because air bends different colours of light by different amounts. East is to the left and north is at the top.

understand.summary: This visible-light composite comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope: the B filter is shown in blue, V in green and hydrogen-alpha in red.
understand.eye: Long exposures build up light the eye cannot gather, so the faint nebulae here would be far too dim to see like this by eye.

alt: A wide star field with bright and dark nebulae and a star cluster on the left.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 2808, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A dense swarm of stars fills this Hubble view of the central region of NGC 2808, a globular cluster in our galaxy. Globular clusters are compact, gravity-bound groups of typically hundreds of thousands of stars, and they were among the earliest settlers of the Milky Way, born as the galaxy itself took shape.

For decades astronomers assumed that all of a cluster's stars formed together, at one time and place and from one batch of material, then aged side by side for billions of years. NGC 2808 upset that picture: Hubble surprised astronomers by finding three generations of stars in it.

All three were born within a span of 200 million years, early in the life of this 12.5-billion-year-old cluster. NGC 2808 is one of the most massive of the roughly 150 known globular clusters in the Milky Way, with more than 1 million stars. The three populations were told apart using Hubble's sharp Advanced Camera for Surveys, which measured the brightness and colours of the cluster's stars.
explore: The cluster lies about 30,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Carina. The Hubble images behind this view were not taken in one go but gathered during several separate observing sessions, a common approach for detailed studies of a single cluster.

understand.summary: This image combines blue, visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and only a view as sharp as Hubble's can separate the crowded stars at the cluster's centre.

alt: A dense swarm of stars in the central region of the globular cluster NGC 2808.

caption: The nebula around the Wolf-Rayet binary star AB7, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Blue bubbles of gas and a small network of green filaments stand out in this ESO view of AB7, one of the most highly excited nebulae in the Magellanic Clouds, the two satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. At its heart is a binary star: a Wolf-Rayet star, which is a highly evolved massive star, paired with a middle-aged massive companion of spectral type O.

Both stars blow exceptionally strong stellar winds, constant outflows of energetic particles, much like our Sun's solar wind, but between 10 and 1,000 million times stronger. These winds press hard on the surrounding interstellar material and sculpt it into bubbles, which show up clearly here by their blue colour.

AB7 stands out even among such stars. The huge nebula around it, together with a region of glowing ionised helium, indicates that its Wolf-Rayet star is among the hottest known, perhaps the hottest, with a surface temperature above 120,000 degrees. The green filaments just outside the nebula are the remains of a supernova explosion.
explore: The view was made with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, using filters that isolate light from helium, oxygen and hydrogen. AB7 lies about 180,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Tucana.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image from the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, taken through filters that isolate light from helium, oxygen and hydrogen. The wind-blown bubbles appear blue, but the colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: These narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and long exposures reveal a nebula far too faint for the eye to see.

alt: A nebula containing blue wind-blown bubbles, with a small network of green filaments just outside it.

caption: The starburst region NGC 3603 in near-infrared light, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This near-infrared view from ESO's Very Large Telescope looks into NGC 3603, a massive region of glowing gas that lies in our galaxy's Carina spiral arm, about 20,000 light-years away. At its centre sits a cluster of hot O- and B-type stars pouring out ultraviolet radiation that ionises the surrounding nebula.

Astronomers call such a place an HII region, because part of its hydrogen is ionised. NGC 3603 is the only massive one in our galaxy where the central ionising cluster can be studied at both visible and near-infrared wavelengths, because the line of sight happens to be fairly clear of dust. Intervening matter dims its near-infrared light only by about a factor of 2, compared with 80 in visible light.

The cluster's more than fifty heavy, bright O stars together have about 100 times the ionising power of the Trapezium cluster in the Orion Nebula. Importantly, the study found plenty of stars with less mass than the Sun, showing that, contrary to several theoretical predictions, low-mass stars do form in violent starbursts.
explore: The hot O and B stars add up to over 2,000 times the mass of the Sun. In many ways the cluster resembles the core of the ionising cluster in the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is about eight times farther away. Young stars still contracting in the innermost region are between 300 000 and 1 000 000 years old.

understand.summary: This image comes from the ISAAC instrument on the VLT's ANTU telescope, taken through three near-infrared filters (Js, H and Ks). The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, but it is dimmed far less by intervening dust than visible light on its way to us.

alt: A near-infrared view of the NGC 3603 region and its central star cluster.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 30, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Messier 30, a globular cluster in which several hundred thousand stars crowd together. It lies about 28,000 light-years from Earth, measures about 90 light-years across, and formed some 13 billion years ago. Charles Messier discovered it in 1764.

Globular clusters like this one are mostly made of old stars. Yet in such a crowded place, some old stars appear to regain their youth, becoming what astronomers call blue stragglers: stars that look hotter and bluer, and so younger, than they ought to.

Using data from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, since retired, researchers identified two kinds of blue stragglers in Messier 30. Some form when stars crash into each other almost head-on. Others live in binary pairs, where the less massive star draws hydrogen fuel away from its heavier partner and is rejuvenated by it.
explore: The picture itself was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, while the blue straggler study relied on the older camera. Messier 30 lies in the direction of the constellation Capricornus, and its crowded core is exactly what makes stellar collisions possible there.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining red and near-infrared exposures. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared data are invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates individual stars packed into this dense swarm.

alt: A dense swarm of stars forming the globular cluster Messier 30.

caption: The region around the star cluster RCW 38, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This wide view from ESO's La Silla Observatory takes in the region around RCW 38, a star cluster about 5,500 light-years away in the direction of Vela, the Sails. It is what astronomers call an embedded cluster: its stars are still wrapped in the cloud of gas and dust from which they formed.

Life there is harsh. Young, giant stars batter nearby fledgling suns and planets with powerful winds and floods of light, aided by massive stars that live fast and end as supernovae. At times this onslaught boils away material that might otherwise have gone on to build new planetary systems.

Scientists think our own Solar System emerged from a similarly dramatic setting, which makes regions like RCW 38 useful for understanding our own origins. An embedded cluster is a snapshot of star formation still under way, before the stars have cleared away the cloud they were born in.
explore: This image comes from the Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on La Silla's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, and combines data taken through four filters: B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha. The field of view is 30 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope combines B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out faint glowing gas around the cluster.

alt: A wide field around the star cluster RCW 38 and its surrounding nebula.

caption: The protostar L1527, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Glowing cavities open above and below a young star in this Webb infrared view, their edges shining orange and blue. The star is the protostar L1527, buried in a cloud of gas and dust that it is feeding on as it grows. Material thrown out by the star has cleared these cavities.

In the upper central region, bubble-like shapes mark stellar 'burps', sporadic ejections from the young star. Webb also picks out filaments of molecular hydrogen that has been shocked by earlier outbursts, a record of the star's restless past.

The shapes are curiously uneven: the cavity edges at upper left and lower right look straight, while those at upper right and lower left curve. The colours carry information too. The lower right region looks blue because there is less dust between it and Webb than in the orange regions above it. Working in infrared lets Webb look into the dusty cloud around the protostar.
explore: L1527 lies about 460 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Taurus. A protostar is a star still in the making, gathering mass from its surroundings before it begins to shine by nuclear fusion in its core.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from Webb's NIRCam: the shortest filter is shown in blue, a filter tracing PAH molecules in green, a molecular hydrogen filter in orange and another long-wavelength filter in red.
understand.eye: This is infrared light, invisible to the eye; the colours are assigned, and here they also hint at how much dust lies in front of each region.

alt: A young star's cloud with glowing cavities above and below it, their boundaries orange and blue, bubble-like shapes in the upper centre and a bluer region at lower right.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 15, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hot blue stars and cooler golden ones swarm together in this Hubble image, crowding ever more densely toward the cluster's bright centre. This is Messier 15, a globular cluster some 35,000 light-years away in the constellation Pegasus, the Winged Horse.

At around 12 billion years old, Messier 15 is one of the oldest globular clusters known. It is also one of the densest, with most of its mass packed into its core. A star's colour is a guide to its surface temperature, which is why the blue and golden stars here are described as hot and cooler.

The cluster holds more than stars. It was the first star cluster found to contain a planetary nebula, the glowing shell of gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star, and a rare type of black hole has been found at its centre. This image combines Hubble observations across ultraviolet, visible and infrared light.
explore: The picture draws on two Hubble instruments: the Wide Field Camera 3 supplied the ultraviolet and blue exposures, and the Advanced Camera for Surveys supplied the visible and near-infrared ones. Combining them captures both the hot blue stars and the cooler golden ones.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys in ultraviolet, visible and infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and infrared parts of this image lie beyond what the eye can see.

alt: A globular cluster of blue and golden stars that grow more crowded toward a bright centre.

caption: The supernova remnant SN 1987A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright ring surrounds the remains of an exploded star at the centre of this Hubble image, set against a backdrop of stars and wrapped in red clouds of gas. This is Supernova 1987A, and the ring is made of material the star threw off about 20 000 years before it exploded.

A supernova remnant is the expanding debris left behind when a massive star blows itself apart. The red colour of the surrounding clouds traces the glow of hydrogen gas. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this image in January 2017, while the colours of the stars in front of and behind the supernova were added from observations with the older Wide Field Planetary Camera 2.

Since its launch in 1990, Hubble has returned to SN 1987A several times, watching its dust cloud expand. Those repeated visits have helped astronomers build a better understanding of these powerful explosions.
explore: SN 1987A lies about 170,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Dorado. The full picture combines blue, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters from two different Hubble cameras.

understand.summary: The central view comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, including a hydrogen-alpha filter, with star colours added from Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 data. The red clouds show glowing hydrogen; the other colour assignments aren't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's long exposures and sharp view reveal a ring and clouds far too small and faint for the eye to make out.

alt: A bright ring around a central exploded star, surrounded by red clouds of gas and a backdrop of stars.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6388, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 6388, a globular cluster in the Milky Way. Like all globular clusters, it formed long ago and is more than ten billion years old. Yet astronomers describe it as dynamically middle-aged.

The distinction is between calendar age and internal evolution. Over time, the heaviest stars in a cluster gradually sink toward its centre. By studying how the cluster's bright blue stars are spread out, researchers found that NGC 6388 has aged at a moderate pace, with its heaviest stars still in the middle of that migration.

Those bright blue stars are blue stragglers, stars that look younger than their neighbours. A study using Hubble data showed that globulars of matching age may have strikingly different distributions of blue stragglers, which suggests that clusters can age at substantially different rates. A cluster's internal clock, in other words, need not match its birthday.
explore: NGC 6388 lies about 35,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Scorpius. The image was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars that would otherwise blur together.

alt: The stars of the globular cluster NGC 6388.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6388, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This view from the Hubble Space Telescope captures NGC 6388, one of the Milky Way's globular clusters, which are ancient, gravity-bound balls of stars. Its stars formed in the distant past, more than ten billion years ago, as is true of every globular cluster.

Even so, astronomers call NGC 6388 dynamically middle-aged. What they mean is how far its internal evolution has progressed. Looking at where its bright blue stars are located, they concluded that it has aged at a moderate speed: its heaviest stars are partway through a slow migration toward the centre.

Those blue stars, known as blue stragglers, appear younger than the stars around them, and because they are relatively heavy they act as tracers of this settling. Hubble data showed that clusters of the same age can differ dramatically in how their blue stragglers are spread out, suggesting that clusters age at markedly different rates.
explore: The cluster lies about 35,000 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. This version of the image was released by ESO and combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view picks out stars that would blur together through an ordinary telescope.

alt: The stars of the globular cluster NGC 6388.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Spikes jut from some of the brighter stars in this ESO image of NGC 6397, a globular cluster about 7,200 light-years away in the southern constellation Ara. Those spikes are not real features of the stars: they appear because the brightest stars overexposed the camera's detector, an effect called CCD bleeding.

Globular clusters are dense, roughly spherical groups of old stars bound by gravity. NGC 6397 has gone through what astronomers call core collapse, and its central region is very dense. In core collapse, encounters between stars gradually drive many of them into a tightly packed centre.
The cluster contains about 400,000 stars. Based on models of how stars evolve, its age is put at 13,400 million years, give or take 800 million, which places it among very old objects indeed.
explore: The image combines B-, V- and I-band exposures from the Wide Field Imager on the 2.2-metre ESO/MPI telescope at La Silla, taken as part of the Pilot Stellar Survey. The ESO Imaging Survey team prepared and supplied the picture.

understand.summary: This composite comes from the Wide Field Imager, using B and V filters in visible light and an I filter in the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the spikes on bright stars are a camera artefact, not something the eye would see.

alt: A dense globular cluster of stars, with spikes extending from some of the brighter stars.

caption: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This ESO image looks into the central part of Omega Centauri, a globular cluster that holds as many as ten million stars. Even this central region covers a patch of sky about as big as the full Moon, roughly half a degree across.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical collection of stars bound together by gravity, and Omega Centauri, also known as NGC 5139, counts its stars in the millions. The picture was captured from ESO's La Silla Observatory with the Wide Field Imager, and it is a colour composite of images taken through three filters known as B, V and I.

There is a small puzzle hidden in the frame. The Wide Field Imager uses a mosaic of detectors, which leaves narrow gaps between them. Two small gaps in this image were patched with lower-quality data from the Digitized Sky Survey, and ESO invites viewers to try to spot them. North is at the top and east is to the left.
explore: The cluster lies about 17,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Centaurus. Its alternative name, NGC 5139, is its number in the New General Catalogue, a long-standing list of nebulae, clusters and galaxies.

understand.summary: This colour composite from the Wide Field Imager combines images taken through B, V and I filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

alt: The dense central part of the globular cluster Omega Centauri, packed with stars.

caption: The massive stars WR 25 and Tr16-244 in the cluster Trumpler 16, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The brightest star in this Hubble image, near the centre, is WR 25; just to its upper left shines Tr16-244, the third brightest. Together they form a pair of colossal stars in the open cluster Trumpler 16. The second-brightest star, to the left of WR 25, is an impostor of sorts: a low-mass star much closer to Earth than the others.

Trumpler 16 is embedded in the Carina Nebula, a vast cauldron of gas and dust about 7500 light-years away in the constellation Carina, the Keel. An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud, and young ones can still be surrounded by the gas from which they were born.

WR 25 is catalogued as a Wolf-Rayet star, a type of massive, highly evolved star that sheds material in powerful winds. Such stars are rare and short-lived, which makes a pair of giants like this in one field worth a close look.
explore: The image was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The foreground star's brightness is a reminder that how bright a star looks depends on its distance as well as its true power.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and, as the second-brightest star here shows, a modest nearby star can outshine a distant giant.

alt: A star field with a very bright star near the centre, another bright star to its left and a third just to its upper left.

caption: The core of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This image from ESO's Very Large Telescope zooms into the central core of 47 Tucanae, a globular cluster about 15,000 light-years away in the constellation Tucana. The frame is 7 arcminutes wide, yet the whole cluster spans about 30 arcminutes on the sky, so this is only its heart.
A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of old stars held together by gravity. Their cores are crowded, so separating the individual stars there calls for a large telescope.

The data were taken with the FORS1 instrument on Kueyen, the second of the VLT's Unit Telescopes, through three filters: U, R and a narrow-band filter centred near 485 nm. The total exposure time was under 5 minutes. The observations were retrieved from the ESO Science Archive; Rubina Kotak processed them and Henri Boffin carried out the final image processing, giving these stored measurements a new life as a picture.
explore: North is at the top and east is to the left. Because the picture was built from observations already held in an archive, it shows how data gathered for one purpose can later be turned into a new image.

understand.summary: This image comes from FORS1 on the VLT's Kueyen telescope, using a U filter at the ultraviolet end of the spectrum, a narrow-band filter near 485 nm and an R filter. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The U filter reaches into ultraviolet light the eye cannot see, and the telescope collects far more light than the eye can.

alt: The crowded central core of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae.

caption: The centre of the globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble has broken the centre of the globular cluster Messier 4 into a multitude of glowing points, each one a star, a colossal nuclear furnace. Lying 7200 light-years away, Messier 4 is relatively close to us, which makes it a prime target for study. Tens of thousands of stars belong to it.

The cluster stands out for its large population of white dwarfs: the exposed cores of old, dying stars that have shed their outer layers into space. It also hosts an unusual planet, PSR B1620-26 b, about 2.5 times the mass of Jupiter, circling a binary pair: a white dwarf together with a pulsar, which is a kind of neutron star. The planet's age is estimated at around 13 billion years, almost three times that of the Solar System.

Since Messier 4 is bright as globular clusters go, amateur stargazers can seek it out with binoculars or a small telescope near the orange-red star Antares in Scorpius. Don't expect Hubble's detail, though: in an eyepiece it looks like a fuzzy ball of light.
explore: Hubble helped make the discovery of the planet PSR B1620-26 b in July 2003. This view was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters, and the cluster is also catalogued as NGC 6121.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars or a small telescope Messier 4 appears only as a fuzzy ball of light; Hubble's sharp view resolves it into individual stars.

scaleExtra: Messier 4 lies about 7200 light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: The centre of a globular cluster resolved into a multitude of glowing stars.

caption: The star cluster NGC 6604 and the nebula Sh2-54, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A bright grouping of stars toward the upper left of this image is the young star cluster NGC 6604. Around it lie the cluster's associated nebula, a cloud of glowing hydrogen gas called Sh2-54, and clouds of dust. The picture was taken by the Wide Field Imager on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The cluster forms the densest part of a looser association of about one hundred brilliant blue-white stars. A stellar association is a widely spread group of young stars that share a common origin but are only weakly held together by gravity, if at all.

Clouds of glowing hydrogen like Sh2-54 typically shine because ultraviolet light from hot young stars makes the gas glow. Together, the cluster, the gas and the dust show a region where stars have recently formed and some of the raw material still remains.
explore: NGC 6604 lies about 5,500 light-years away in the direction of Serpens Cauda. The image combines five filters spanning ultraviolet and visible light, including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines U, B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters, from the ultraviolet end of the spectrum through visible light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and a hydrogen-alpha filter bring out faint glowing gas that the eye could not see directly.

alt: A bright group of stars at upper left amid a cloud of glowing hydrogen gas and dust clouds.

caption: The star cluster R136 in the Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble looks here into the heart of the Tarantula Nebula, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud. At lower right sits R136, a young, dense star cluster packed with hundreds of young blue stars. Among them is the most massive star yet detected in the Universe.
