Using Hubble, astronomers studied the central, densest part of R136 in detail and found nine stars each weighing more than 100 times the mass of the Sun. The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way, and the Tarantula Nebula within it is a vast cloud of gas where new stars are forming.

Stars of such enormous mass are rare and burn through their fuel quickly, so finding a group of them together offers a valuable chance to learn how the most massive stars form and live. Hubble's sharp view is what makes it possible to separate them in such a crowded cluster.
explore: R136 lies about 170,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Dorado. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through filters ranging from ultraviolet to near-infrared, including one that isolates glowing hydrogen.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet or near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharpness separates individual stars in a crowded cluster in another galaxy.

alt: The central Tarantula Nebula, with a dense cluster of blue stars at lower right.

caption: The star cluster Trumpler 14, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A prominent dark patch sits close to the centre of this Hubble view of the star cluster Trumpler 14. It is a Bok globule: a small, isolated dark nebula containing dense dust and gas, seen against the stars around it.

Few places in the Milky Way gather as many hot, massive, bright stars as Trumpler 14, and it contains several of the most luminous stars found anywhere in our galaxy. Massive stars are short-lived and pour out intense light, which makes clusters like this natural places to study stellar heavyweights.

Bok globules remain a subject of active research, because their internal structure and density are still something of a mystery. Dark nebulae like this one are visible only because they block the light of stars or glowing gas behind them, so they appear as shadows rather than shining objects.
explore: Trumpler 14 lies about 8000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Carina. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible, red and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible, red and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the dark globule is seen only because it blocks light from behind it.

alt: A cluster of bright stars with a prominent dark patch near its centre.

caption: The star cluster Pismis 24 in the nebula NGC 6357, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The bright stars in this Hubble image belong to Pismis 24, a small open cluster sitting at the heart of NGC 6357, a large emission nebula, in the direction of Scorpius. The nebula spans one degree on the sky. Intense ultraviolet light from the cluster's hottest stars heats the surrounding gas and has blown a bubble in the nebula.

Pismis 24-1, a bright young star in the cluster's core about 8,000 light-years from Earth, had been one of the leading candidates for the Milky Way's heaviest star. It was thought to weigh an astonishing 200 to 300 times as much as the Sun.

New Hubble measurements changed that picture. They resolved Pismis 24-1 into two separate stars, which roughly halved its mass estimate to around 100 solar masses. The cluster's youngest, bluest heavyweights ionise part of the nebula, and the surrounding gas clouds make the region harder to study.
explore: An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that glows because nearby hot stars energise it. This image combines data from two Hubble cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, including filters that isolate glowing hydrogen.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, using visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view split what looked like one star into two, a separation far beyond what the eye could make.

alt: A group of bright stars in the core of a glowing nebula.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 3766, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: These young stars make up NGC 3766, an open star cluster, in the constellation Centaurus, the Centaur. ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile took the picture.

An open cluster is a loose family of stars born together from the same cloud of gas, so its members share a similar age and origin. That makes clusters like this a useful place to compare stars that started out under the same conditions.

NGC 3766 has turned out to hold a surprise. A team from the Geneva Observatory watched its stars very carefully with the Swiss 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope, also at La Silla, and found that 36 of them belong to a new and previously unknown class of variable star. Variable stars are stars whose brightness changes over time, and each class tells astronomers something different about what goes on inside them.
explore: NGC 3766 lies about 7000 light-years away. The colour image was built from exposures through B, V and I filters taken with the telescope's Wide Field Imager, spanning visible light into the near-infrared.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope combines B, V and I filters, spanning visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the subtle brightness changes of variable stars can only be found with careful measurements over time.

alt: A group of young stars forming the open cluster NGC 3766.

caption: The nebula NGC 1788 in Orion, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A delicate, ghostly cloud glows in this finely detailed ESO image. This is the nebula NGC 1788, which lies about 3000 light-years away in a dark and often overlooked corner of the constellation Orion, somewhat isolated from Orion's bright stars.

Isolation does not mean independence. The powerful winds and light of those bright stars strongly affect the nebula, sculpting its shape and helping to make it home to a multitude of infant stars. NGC 1788 is catalogued as a reflection nebula: a cloud of dust that shines mainly by scattering the light of nearby stars.

Nebulae like this show how star birth in one place can be shaped by stars elsewhere. Radiation and winds travel across space, pressing on gas and dust and influencing where and how new stars form, even in a quiet corner of the sky.
explore: Taken with La Silla's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and its Wide Field Imager, the picture combines blue, green and red filters with a special filter tuned to the glow of hydrogen gas. The frame spans about 30 arcminutes, with north up and east to the left.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines blue, green and red filters with one that isolates glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, revealing a faint nebula that would be hard to see directly.

alt: A faint, delicate nebula in a dark region of sky.

caption: The open star cluster Messier 7, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Messier 7, a bright star cluster also catalogued as NGC 6475, is the subject of this view from the Wide Field Imager at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. It lies about 800 light-years away, in the direction of the tail of Scorpius, the Scorpion.

Messier 7 is easy to spot with the naked eye and ranks among the most prominent open clusters in the sky. An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust and only weakly held together by gravity; over time such clusters tend to drift apart.

Because the stars of an open cluster share a common age and distance, differences between them reveal how stars of different masses evolve. That is one reason Messier 7 is an important target for research as well as an easy sight for skywatchers.
explore: The image combines exposures through B, V and I filters, spanning visible light into the near-infrared. Although the cluster is plain to the naked eye, a camera on a large telescope records far fainter stars in the surrounding field.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope combines B, V and I filters, from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Messier 7 is visible to the naked eye, but the camera's long exposures reveal many fainter stars, and the I-band light is invisible to the eye.

alt: The bright open star cluster Messier 7.

caption: The open cluster NGC 4755, known as the Jewel Box, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: The star cluster NGC 4755, widely known as the Jewel Box, sits among rich, multicoloured surroundings in this wide view from ESO's La Silla Observatory. The picture comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and spans 20 arcminutes of sky.

NGC 4755 is an open cluster lying about 6500 light-years away in the direction of Crux. Open clusters are groups of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Because their members share a common age, they help astronomers compare how stars of different masses develop.

Stars shine in different colours because their surfaces have different temperatures: hotter stars look bluer, cooler ones redder. A wide field like this one places the cluster in context, showing its rich surroundings as well as the cluster itself.
explore: The picture is based on images taken through B, V and I filters, covering visible light and the near-infrared. Its wide field shows the cluster together with its surroundings rather than in isolation.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and I filters, from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the long exposures bring out far fainter stars than the eye could see.

alt: A star cluster surrounded by a rich, multicoloured field of stars.

caption: The globular star cluster NGC 6752, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This view from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager at La Silla shows NGC 6752, a globular star cluster in the southern constellation Pavo, the Peacock, about 14,000 light-years away.

Globular clusters are dense, ball-shaped groups of old stars held together by gravity. Because their stars formed at roughly the same time, they are natural laboratories for testing ideas about how stars age and die.

NGC 6752 delivered a surprise. Studies of the cluster with ESO's Very Large Telescope unexpectedly showed that many of its stars do not go through a phase of mass loss at the end of their lives. Ageing stars are generally expected to shed material into space as they near the end, so the finding challenges the standard picture of how such stars finish their lives.
explore: The picture combines exposures through two filters, B and V, both in visible light. It was taken with a wide-field camera at La Silla, while the study of the stars' mass loss relied on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager uses B and V filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, revealing individual stars across the cluster.

alt: The globular star cluster NGC 6752, a dense ball of stars.

caption: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image looks into Omega Centauri, which is both the biggest and the brightest of the sky's globular clusters. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars held together by gravity, and Omega Centauri has long posed puzzles for astronomers.

A discovery has now resolved part of that mystery. Images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, together with measurements from the GMOS spectrograph at Chile's Gemini South telescope, suggest that the cluster seems to hide a hard-to-find intermediate-mass black hole in its core.

Intermediate-mass black holes are thought to bridge the gap between the black holes left by single stars and the supermassive ones found at the hearts of large galaxies. They have proved hard to find, which is why a candidate in a cluster within our own galaxy attracts attention. Like any black hole, it cannot be seen directly; its presence has to be inferred from its effect on its surroundings.
explore: Omega Centauri lies about 17,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Centaurus, and it is also catalogued as NGC 5139. The black hole result drew on two very different instruments: a camera in space and a spectrograph on the ground.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and red filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view separates individual stars in the crowded cluster, while the black hole itself is invisible and can only be detected through its influence.

alt: The crowded stars of the globular cluster Omega Centauri.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 3532, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Stars of contrasting colours fill this vivid view of NGC 3532, a bright star cluster. Some still shine with a hot bluish light, while many of the heavier ones have already swollen into red giants and glow a rich orange.

The difference tells a story about age. A star's colour reflects its surface temperature, and the most massive stars run through their fuel fastest. In a cluster whose stars were born together, the heaviest ones are therefore the first to swell into cool red giants, while less massive stars carry on shining much as before.

NGC 3532 is an open cluster, a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud, lying about 1300 light-years away in the direction of Carina. The picture was captured with La Silla's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope in Chile.
explore: The image combines exposures through B, V and I filters, reaching from visible light into the near-infrared, plus a hydrogen-alpha filter that isolates the red glow of hydrogen gas in the field.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, spanning visible light and the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the long exposures show far more stars than the eye could see.

alt: A bright star cluster of bluish and orange stars.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6362, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This colourful view shows NGC 6362, a brilliant ball of ancient stars in the southern constellation Ara, the Altar. It was recorded at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile by the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope.

NGC 6362 is a globular cluster lying about 25,000 light-years away. Globular clusters are dense, roughly spherical collections of stars bound tightly by gravity, and their stars are typically very old, formed early in the history of their galaxy.

Because nearly all their stars formed at about the same time, globular clusters act as fossils, preserving a record of conditions long ago. Differences in colour among their stars largely reflect differences in temperature and in how far each star has progressed through its life.
explore: The picture combines exposures through B, V and I filters, spanning visible light into the near-infrared. A wide-field camera like this one can capture the whole cluster and its surroundings in a single view.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and I filters, from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the long exposures separate stars the eye could never pick out.

alt: A colourful, brilliant ball of ancient stars.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 2547, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Bright stars of the open cluster NGC 2547 are scattered across this image from ESO's La Silla Observatory. Look between them, far in the background, and many remote galaxies appear, some clearly spiral in shape.

NGC 2547 lies about 1500 light-years away in the direction of Vela, well inside our own galaxy. The galaxies behind it are separate systems far beyond the Milky Way, so this single frame spans an enormous range of distances, from nearby stars to faraway galaxies.

An open cluster is a loose group of young stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Their shared age and distance make such clusters useful for studying how stars develop. The image was taken with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager.
explore: The picture combines exposures through B, V and R filters, all in visible light. Long exposures of a nearby cluster also reveal much fainter objects far beyond it, such as the background galaxies seen here.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out remote galaxies far too faint to see directly.

alt: Bright stars of an open cluster, with many faint, distant galaxies in the background, some of them spiral-shaped.

caption: Debris from an explosive star birth in the Orion Molecular Cloud, imaged by ALMA, Gemini South and ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This composite view of the Orion Nebula complex captures firework-like debris, with the well-known Trapezium Cluster of hot, young stars near the bottom. The debris is what remains of an explosion some 500 years ago, set off as a group of massive stars was being born.

Stellar explosions usually bring to mind supernovae, the violent deaths of stars. These new ALMA observations show that the other end of a star's life cycle, its birth, can also be violent and explosive.

The colours in the ALMA data come from carbon monoxide gas and encode motion through the Doppler shift. Blue marks gas rushing toward us at the highest speeds, while red marks gas approaching more slowly. The Doppler effect changes the wavelength of light from a moving source, so it reveals how fast gas is moving along our line of sight.
explore: The background combines optical and near-infrared images from the Gemini South telescope and ESO's Very Large Telescope, and the ALMA data do not cover the whole frame. The Orion Molecular Cloud lies about 1400 light-years away.

understand.summary: ALMA's millimetre observations of carbon monoxide are colour-coded by speed: blue for gas approaching fastest, red for gas approaching more slowly. The background is optical and near-infrared imaging from Gemini South and the VLT.
understand.eye: The millimetre-wavelength and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the blue and red here encode speeds, not colours anyone would see.

alt: A composite view of part of the Orion Nebula complex with blue and red firework-like debris and a cluster of stars towards the bottom.

caption: The globular cluster 47 Tucanae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, also called NGC 104, which belongs to the constellation Tucana, the Toucan, in the southern sky. It hosts tens of thousands of stars and, it is second only to Omega Centauri in brightness among the night sky's globular clusters.

Scientists used Hubble to study the cluster's white dwarfs, the faint remnants of dying stars. These stars move out from the crowded centre of the cluster toward its outskirts. Astronomers already knew the process should happen, but it had never been seen in action until this detailed study of 47 Tucanae.

In crowded clusters, gravitational encounters between stars tend to sort them by mass over time, with heavier stars settling inward and lighter ones spreading outward. Watching white dwarfs travel outward offers a direct look at how a cluster rearranges its stars.
explore: 47 Tucanae lies about 15,000 light-years away. The image combines ultraviolet data from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 with visible and near-infrared data from its Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: This image combines ultraviolet light from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 with visible and near-infrared light from its Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared data lie beyond what the eye can see, and Hubble's sharp view separates the individual stars of this crowded cluster.

alt: A dense globular cluster packed with stars.

caption: The star-forming region Messier 17, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This near-infrared view from ESO's Very Large Telescope looks into the sky region of Messier 17, a glowing cloud of gas energised by a cluster of young, hot stars. Astronomers call such a place an H II region: a cloud in which hydrogen has been ionised by the intense ultraviolet light of hot young stars.

The notable find here lies to the south-west of the cluster's centre: a large disc seen in silhouette. Discs of gas and dust are thought to form around young stars, and seeing one in silhouette lets astronomers trace its outline against the brighter background.

Near-infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light, which helps in dusty star-forming regions like this one. The image was made with the ISAAC instrument on ANTU, one of the 8.2-metre telescopes of the VLT at Paranal.
explore: Messier 17 lies about 5500 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. This is a three-colour composite built from J, H and K filters, and it covers a field about six arcminutes across.

understand.summary: This is a three-colour near-infrared composite from ISAAC on the VLT, using J, H and K filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it reveals structure in dusty regions that visible light cannot penetrate as well.

alt: A near-infrared view of the Messier 17 region, with a silhouetted disc south-west of the cluster centre.

caption: The Herbig-Haro object HH 110, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Herbig-Haro 110, a geyser of hot gas streaming away from a newborn star. Herbig-Haro objects are glowing patches that form where jets of material shot out by young stars slam into the surrounding gas and dust.

HH 110 is unusual. Most Herbig-Haro objects come in pairs, marking jets that shoot out in opposite directions, but this one appears on its own. Astronomers suspect it could be the extension of a second object, HH 270, whose flow has been deflected after striking a dense cloud of gas.

If that idea is right, HH 110 shows how the outflows of young stars can interact with their surroundings, changing course when they meet denser material. Hubble's view combines visible and infrared light, including a filter that picks out glowing hydrogen.
explore: HH 110 lies about 1500 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Orion. The picture combines data from two Hubble cameras: the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: This image combines a hydrogen-alpha filter from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with visible and near-infrared filters from Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared data are invisible to the eye, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hot gas in the jet.

alt: A jet of glowing gas flowing from a newborn star.

caption: The region around the young star MWC 147 in Monoceros, imaged from ESO's Paranal Observatory with a 200 mm lens
story: The rich, colourful region around the Cone Nebula sits at centre left of this wide-field image, with the Rosette Nebula at top right. Both lie in the constellation Monoceros, very close to the better-known Orion. The view takes in the star-forming complex NGC 2247 and the young star MWC 147.

MWC 147 sits near a dark nebula in the upper left part of the frame. It is classed as a Herbig Ae/Be object, a young star still in its formative stages, and it belongs to Monoceros OB1, an association of massive stars. A dark nebula is a dense cloud of dust that blocks light from behind it.

This picture was not taken with a large observatory telescope. Stéphane Guisard of ESO photographed it from Paranal with a 200 mm lens, combining exposures through R, V, B and hydrogen-alpha filters for a total of more than 16 hours. That long total exposure is what brings out the faint glow of the nebulae.
explore: MWC 147 lies about 2500 light-years away. Grouping massive stars into associations such as Monoceros OB1 helps astronomers trace which stars formed together from the same clouds of gas and dust.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light colour composite made with a 200 mm camera lens, using R, V, B and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: More than 16 hours of total exposure gather far more light than the eye can, revealing nebulae far too faint to see like this unaided.

alt: A wide field of sky with a colourful nebula region at centre left, another nebula at top right and a dark nebula at top left.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 70, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The compact, brilliant centre of the globular cluster Messier 70 fills this Hubble image, the cluster growing steadily brighter toward its middle. Globular clusters are tight quarters: gravity binds hundreds of thousands of stars into a small region of space.

Messier 70 is special because it has undergone core collapse. As stars in a cluster interact over time, lighter ones tend to speed up and wander toward the edges, while heavier ones slow down and gather in orbits near the centre. That huddling creates the dense, bright cores typical of core-collapsed clusters. Of the Milky Way's more than 150 globulars, roughly one in five has been through it.

While many globular clusters live in the galaxy's outskirts, this one circles near the heart of the Milky Way, around 30 000 light-years from the Solar System. That it has stayed intact despite the strong gravitational pull of the galactic hub.
explore: Just about 68 light-years wide, Messier 70 can be glimpsed, very faintly, with binoculars under dark skies in Sagittarius. Charles Messier logged it in 1780, making it number seventy in his famous list. The picture comes from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and covers about 3.3 by 3.3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars Messier 70 is only very faintly visible; Hubble resolves the individual stars of its crowded core.

alt: The bright, compact centre of a globular cluster, growing brighter toward the middle.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 56, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble has resolved Messier 56 (NGC 6779), a globular cluster, into a multitude of individual stars, tightly bound together by gravity. It lies about 33 000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Lyra, the Lyre.

Charles Messier did not know it was made of stars when he first observed it. His telescope could not separate them, so it looked like a fuzzy ball, and he described it as 'a nebula without stars'. Studying such a cluster is tricky, because it lies near the plane of our galaxy, where unrelated field stars in the same direction can contaminate its light.

By comparing Hubble's observations with the standard theory of stellar evolution, astronomers estimate that the cluster is about 13 billion years old. Its stars hold comparatively little of any element beyond hydrogen and helium, which points to a birth early in the Universe's history. Most clusters with a similar chemistry are lined up along a plane in the Milky Way's halo, which suggests they were taken from a satellite galaxy instead of being the galaxy's own oldest clusters.
explore: Astronomers study clusters like this with the colour-magnitude, or Hertzsprung-Russell, diagram, which compares stars' brightness and colour and so reveals their surface temperatures. Gilles Chapdelaine entered a version of this image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through Messier's telescope this cluster looked like a fuzzy ball; Hubble separates it into individual stars, partly using near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A globular cluster resolved into many individual stars.

caption: The Wild Duck Cluster, Messier 11, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Blue stars gather at the centre of this image, surrounded by a scattering of redder ones. The blue stars are the young, hot members of the Wild Duck Cluster, an open cluster also catalogued as Messier 11. The redder stars around them are older, cooler stars lying in the background.

A star's colour is a guide to its temperature: hotter stars shine bluer, cooler ones redder. So the colour contrast here helps separate the cluster from the unrelated stars behind it, which simply happen to lie in the same direction.

Open clusters are groups of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust, so their members share an age. The Wild Duck Cluster lies about 6000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Scutum. The picture was taken with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager at La Silla in Chile.
explore: The picture combines exposures through B, V and I filters, reaching from visible light into the near-infrared. Together the filters bring out both the hot blue cluster members and the cooler, redder stars that lie far behind them.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and I filters, from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The blue and red star colours reflect real differences in temperature, but the I-band data are near-infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A cluster of blue stars at the centre, surrounded by redder background stars.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 53, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands upon thousands of brilliant stars make up Messier 53, the globular cluster in this Hubble image. Bound tightly by gravity, it is roughly spherical and grows denser toward its heart.

Such clusters are far from rare; more than 150 exist in the Milky Way. Messier 53 lies on the outer edges of our galaxy, roughly as far from the galactic centre as it is from the Sun. William Herschel, not known for poetic flourishes, once counted a globular cluster among the most beautiful sights he could recall in the heavens.

Messier 53 holds a surprise: an unusual number of blue stragglers. Because all of a globular cluster's stars are expected to form at about the same time, they should follow a trend set by the cluster's age and their masses. Blue stragglers break that rule, looking brighter and younger than they should. Their exact nature is still a mystery, but they most likely arise when stars in the packed centre pass very close to each other or even collide.
explore: Messier 53, also catalogued as NGC 5024, lies about 60,000 light-years away in Coma Berenices. Since globulars are far older and bigger than open clusters, astronomers expect them to contain fewer massive blue stars and more old red ones. The picture combines visible and infrared exposures from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel and spans about 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates thousands of individual stars.

alt: A roughly spherical cluster of thousands of brilliant stars, growing denser toward its centre.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6934, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright spray of stars fills this Hubble image of NGC 6934, a globular cluster in the small constellation Delphinus, the Dolphin. Globular clusters are big balls of ancient stars, usually a few hundred thousand of them, found on the outskirts of galaxies.

Lying 50 000 light-years away in the Milky Way's outer reaches, NGC 6934 holds some of the most distant stars still belonging to our galaxy: a far-flung suburb of the galactic city. William Herschel first saw it in the late eighteenth century, but he could not resolve it into stars and classed it as a 'bright nebula'.

The cluster is invisible to the naked eye and very hard to see even with binoculars, yet amateur astronomers like it because fairly inexpensive telescopes show it easily. Its faintness comes from its distance, not a lack of stars: it holds many thousands. Patrick Moore included it in his Caldwell catalogue of objects for amateurs to seek out.
explore: For more than 50 years Moore presented The Sky at Night on BBC TV. This picture was built from two filters, one near-infrared and one orange, with exposures of 29 minutes each, and it covers a field 3.3 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: the near-infrared filter (F814W) is shown in red and the orange filter (F606W) in blue.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the cluster itself is too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A bright spray of stars forming the globular cluster NGC 6934.

caption: The young star cluster NGC 6611 in the Eagle Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Dazzling stars scattered across a section of the Eagle Nebula make up NGC 6611 in this Hubble image, with dark patches punctuating the stellar landscape. NGC 6611 is an open star cluster about 6500 light-years from Earth, whose stars formed about 5.5 million years ago.

It is a very young cluster, full of hot blue stars whose fierce ultraviolet light makes the surrounding nebula glow. Astronomers call places like this HII regions, after the ionised hydrogen that makes up most of them. In the far future the region will disperse, helped along by shock waves from supernovae as its more massive young stars end their short lives.

The dark patches are not empty. They are very dense clouds of gas and dust that block light, and many may hide the early stages of star formation, before young stars clear their surroundings and emerge into view.
explore: The picture used an unusual pairing of two near-infrared filters, each exposed for 2000 seconds, and a ground-based image through more standard filters added a subtle touch of colour. The frame spans about 3.2 arcminutes. From a dark site, huge dark nebulae can be seen against the Milky Way with the naked eye.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using two near-infrared filters: F775W shown in blue and F850LP in red, with subtle extra colour from a ground-based image.
understand.eye: Both Hubble filters record light at or beyond the red limit of human vision, so the colours here are a translation rather than what the eye would see.

alt: Bright stars of a young cluster scattered across part of a nebula, with dark patches of dust among them.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 4147, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4147, a globular cluster lying about 60 000 light-years away in Coma Berenices, a northern constellation whose name means Berenice's Hair. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of old stars held together by gravity.

NGC 4147 played a part in a larger project. It was one of many globular clusters that astronomers used to work out how much mass the Milky Way holds in total. In general, the way objects orbit a galaxy depends on how much mass pulls on them, so tracking distant clusters offers a way to weigh the whole system.

Much of a galaxy's mass is thought to lie in forms that do not shine, so measurements like this rely on indirect tracers. Far-off clusters such as NGC 4147 are useful because they sample the galaxy's gravity well away from its bright centre.
explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visible and near-infrared filters. Hubble's sharp view separates the cluster's crowded stars individually, which is what makes such a distant object useful for precise measurements.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and a cluster this distant needs a powerful telescope to be seen as individual stars.

alt: A globular cluster of densely packed stars.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 68, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars crowd together in this Hubble view of Messier 68, a globular cluster: a spherical, star-filled region of space. In such clusters, the shared gravitational pull of hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of stars lets them survive as a group for many billions of years.

Astronomers can read a cluster's age in the light of its stars. Chemical elements leave signatures in starlight, and globular cluster stars usually contain less carbon, oxygen, iron and other heavy elements than stars like the Sun. Because successive generations of stars build up these elements through nuclear fusion, stars poor in them are relics of earlier times. Globular cluster stars rank among the oldest known, at more than 10 billion years.

More than 150 globular clusters surround the Milky Way, and on a galactic scale they are small. Messier 68's stars fill a volume little more than a hundred light-years across, while the Milky Way's disc stretches some 100 000 light-years or more.
explore: About 33 000 light-years from Earth, Messier 68 sits in the constellation Hydra, the Female Water Snake, and was the sixty-eighth entry in Charles Messier's catalogue. The image combines visible and infrared light from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and covers about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Camera of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates the cluster's crowded stars.

alt: A crowded, spherical cluster of stars.

caption: The stellar cluster Terzan 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view peers through the thick dust clouds of our galaxy's central bulge to reveal Terzan 5, a stellar cluster with an unusual mix of stars. An international team of astronomers studied that mix and reached a striking conclusion about the cluster's origins.

Their results indicate that Terzan 5 is not an ordinary cluster but one of the original building blocks of the bulge, probably left over from the Milky Way's earliest days. The bulge is the dense, crowded region of stars around the centre of our galaxy, and working out how it was assembled is a key part of understanding the Milky Way's history.

The observations drew on several telescopes: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, the Multi-conjugate Adaptive Optics Demonstrator (MAD) on ESO's Very Large Telescope, and the second-generation Near Infrared Camera at the Keck Telescope. Infrared light helps here, because it passes through dust that blocks much of the visible light from this region.
explore: Terzan 5 lies about 20,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. This image combines visible and near-infrared filters from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with near-infrared data from Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye and passes through dust that dims this cluster in visible light.

alt: A dense stellar cluster seen through the dusty central region of the Milky Way.

caption: The supernova remnant 1E 0102.2-7219 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Blue wisps of gas near the centre of this Hubble image form the supernova remnant 1E 0102.2-7219, while part of N 76 (also called Henize 1956), a massive star-forming region, glows green and pink at lower right. The scene lies in the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of our nearest neighbouring galaxies.

A supernova remnant is the expanding cloud of debris left behind when a massive star explodes. This picture sets the scene for a search for an elusive missing object hidden in a complex tangle of gaseous filaments: a neutron star, the ultra-dense collapsed core that such an explosion can leave behind.

Finding such a remnant core is difficult, because a neutron star is tiny and faint compared with the glowing gas around it. Hubble's wide range of filters, from ultraviolet to near-infrared, helps separate the different gases in the scene.
explore: The Small Magellanic Cloud lies in the direction of the constellation Tucana. This image draws on two Hubble cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, and on many filters that isolate light from specific elements such as oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and sulphur.

understand.summary: This image combines many filters from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, from ultraviolet to near-infrared, including ones that isolate glowing oxygen, hydrogen and sulphur. The remnant's gas appears blue, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Several of these filters capture ultraviolet or near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases.

alt: Blue wisps of gas near the centre and a green and pink star-forming region at lower right.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 3, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Messier 3, a globular cluster containing an incredible half a million stars. About eight billion years old, it ranks among the biggest and brightest globulars yet found.

Its real distinction is a remarkable number of variable stars, which change in brightness over time: 274 so far, far more than any other globular cluster, with more still turning up. At least 170 are RR Lyrae variables, whose pulsation period is linked to their true brightness. Comparing true and apparent brightness gives their distance, so they serve as standard candles.

The cluster also holds a relatively high number of blue stragglers, which show up clearly in this image. They appear youthful, outshining their neighbours and looking bluer, yet all of a globular cluster's stars are thought to have formed together. One explanation is that an old star gains mass, for example by stripping it from a nearby star, which turns it bluer and makes it seem younger than it is.
explore: Messier 3 lies about 34,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Canes Venatici. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the brightness changes of variable stars only reveal themselves through repeated measurements.

alt: A dense globular cluster of stars, including a number of conspicuous blue stars.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula and its surroundings in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Star clusters, glowing clouds of gas and the scattered remains of supernova explosions spread across this detailed view from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. The main attraction is the Tarantula Nebula, glowing brightly in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
About 160 000 light-years away, the Tarantula is the Large Magellanic Cloud's most spectacular feature. This picture shows not only the nebula itself but also its rich surroundings in great detail.

A nebula like this is a vast cloud of gas and dust where new stars form, and hot young stars make the gas glow. Supernova remnants are the expanding debris of massive stars that have exploded, so the scene mixes stellar birth and stellar death in a single frame.
explore: The image was built with OmegaCAM, the survey telescope's camera, from exposures through several filters, including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen. The field lies in the direction of the constellation Dorado.

understand.summary: This image from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope combines g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters, covering visible light and the edge of the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal glowing gas in another galaxy in far more detail than the eye could ever see.

scaleExtra: The Tarantula Nebula lies about 160 000 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A wide landscape of star clusters, glowing gas clouds and supernova remains around the Tarantula Nebula.

caption: The light echo around the star V838 Monocerotis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Swirling spirals of dust sweep across this Hubble image, lit by a red supergiant star at its middle. The star is V838 Monocerotis, and the glowing pattern is an expanding halo of light spreading into the interstellar dust around it. The resemblance to Vincent van Gogh's 'Starry Night', with its bold whorls of light, is striking.

The illumination comes from a flashbulb-like pulse of light that the star gave off two years before this picture was taken. As that light travels outward, it lights up successive parts of the surrounding dust, revealing spirals never seen before across trillions of kilometres of space. This effect is known as a light echo.

Van Gogh's sky came only from his imagination, but here nature produced something similar. V838 Mon lies about 20,000 light-years from Earth in the direction of Monoceros, which puts it on the outer edge of our galaxy.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this image on February 8, 2004, and at the time it was the telescope's latest look at the star's expanding halo. Repeated views like this let astronomers follow the light as it moves outward through the dust.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The dust is visible only because it reflects the star's earlier outburst, and the faint halo would be far too dim to see without a large telescope.

alt: Swirling spirals of illuminated dust around a red star at the centre.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 12, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars crowd into this Hubble image of Messier 12, a globular cluster whose high concentration of stars makes it a fine photographic subject. Its distance is about 23 000 light-years, in the direction of Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. The calm appearance is deceptive: this cluster seems to have had a violent past.

Crowded quarters in globular clusters can create exotic binary systems, in which two stars are locked in tight orbits and one devours matter from the other, giving off X-rays. Such X-ray binaries are thought to form in very close stellar encounters, and even though Messier 12 is fairly spread out for a globular cluster, X-ray sources have been found in it.

Messier 12 also has far fewer low-mass stars than expected. Using ESO's Very Large Telescope, astronomers gauged how bright and what colour more than 16 000 of its 200 000 stars are. Their speculation is that close to one million low-mass stars were pulled away as the cluster passed through the densest parts of the Milky Way on its orbit around the galactic centre.
explore: The image was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel. Exposure times were 1360 seconds through the blue filter, 200 seconds through the red filter and 364 seconds in the near-infrared, and the frame spans about 3.2 by 3.1 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a blue filter (F435W) is shown in blue, a red filter (F625W) in green and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and the red filter is displayed as green, so the colours are not exactly those the eye would perceive.

alt: A crowded globular cluster of stars.

caption: The young star cluster RCW 38, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Dark tendrils of dust thread through the bright core of the young star cluster RCW 38 in this view from ESO's Very Large Telescope, and clouds of brightly glowing gas surround the cluster. The picture shows the region in exquisite detail.

The image was taken while testing the HAWK-I camera together with the GRAAL adaptive optics system. Adaptive optics measures how Earth's turbulent atmosphere blurs incoming light and corrects for it in real time, so a ground-based telescope can produce much sharper images than it otherwise could.

HAWK-I works in near-infrared light, which passes through dust more easily than visible light. That is an advantage in a young cluster like RCW 38, where dust threads through the region, as the dark tendrils show.
explore: RCW 38 lies in the direction of the constellation Vela. The image combines three near-infrared filters, J, H and Ks, and covers a field about eight arcminutes across. Test observations like this check that new instruments work as designed before regular science begins.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from the HAWK-I camera on the VLT, working with the GRAAL adaptive optics system and using J, H and Ks filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and adaptive optics undoes much of the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere.

alt: A young star cluster surrounded by brightly glowing gas, with dark tendrils of dust running through its bright core.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 15 and the planetary nebula Pease 1, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Dazzling stars fill this Hubble image of Messier 15, and they look fresh and new. In fact they are all roughly 13 billion years old, among the most ancient objects in the Universe. To the lower left of the cluster's core, a small blue blob marks Pease 1, a planetary nebula.

As a globular cluster, Messier 15 is a ball-shaped gathering of old stars born together out of a single gas cloud. It sits in the halo, the outer reaches of the Milky Way, orbiting the Galactic Centre about 35 000 light-years from Earth in Pegasus. Few known globulars are as dense, and most of its mass is packed into the core. Astronomers think such dense clusters went through core collapse, in which gravitational interactions drew many stars toward the centre.

Messier 15 was the first globular cluster known to host a planetary nebula, and it remains one of just four such clusters. A planetary nebula is the glowing shell of gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star.
explore: Unlike the unusually sparse cluster Palomar 1, featured in another Hubble Picture of the Week, Messier 15 remains rich and bright in spite of its great age. The image comes from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel, with exposures of 535 and 615 seconds, and spans 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a yellow/orange filter (F606W) is shown in blue and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the colours are reassigned, so the image does not show the stars' natural hues.

alt: A dense cluster of bright stars with a small blue blob to the lower left of its core.

caption: The star cluster NGC 1850 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Reddish filaments surround a cluster of thousands of stars in this image. The cluster is NGC 1850, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbour of the Milky Way, roughly 160 000 light-years away. The filaments are vast clouds of hydrogen, believed to be the remains of supernova explosions.

The picture overlays two sets of visible-light observations. ESO's Very Large Telescope captured the wide field and the filaments, while the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope imaged the central cluster.

Among its many stars, NGC 1850 hosts a black hole with 11 times the Sun's mass, circled by a star of five solar masses. Astronomers inferred the black hole's presence from the star's orbit, using the MUSE instrument at the VLT; it was the first small black hole beyond the Milky Way to be discovered by this method. Black holes give off no light of their own, so watching how they tug on companions is one of the few ways to find them.
explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud lies in the direction of the constellation Dorado. The filters used include ones that isolate the red glow of hydrogen, on both the VLT's FORS1 instrument and Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light overlay combining FORS1 on the VLT with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, including hydrogen-alpha filters. The hydrogen filaments appear reddish, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The black hole itself is invisible; its presence was inferred only from the motion of a star around it.

scaleExtra: NGC 1850 lies roughly 160 000 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A cluster of thousands of stars surrounded by reddish filaments of gas.

caption: The globular star cluster Messier 55, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: This infrared view from the VISTA survey telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile shows Messier 55, a globular star cluster in the constellation Sagittarius, the Archer. This vast ball of ancient stars lies about 17 000 light-years from Earth.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical group of stars bound together by gravity. Its stars are typically very old, formed early in the history of their galaxy, which makes clusters like this valuable records of the distant past.

VISTA is a survey telescope, built to map large areas of sky, and it works in infrared light. Infrared passes through interstellar dust more easily than visible light and is especially good at picking up cooler stars, so an infrared view of a cluster can look quite different from a visible-light one.
explore: The image combines two infrared filters, Y and H, from VISTA's camera, VIRCAM, and covers a field about 17 arcminutes across. VISTA's full name is the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy.

understand.summary: This is an infrared image from the VIRCAM camera on ESO's VISTA telescope, using Y and H filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours are a translation of light we cannot see.

alt: The globular cluster Messier 55, a vast ball of stars, seen in infrared light.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 107, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's view of Messier 107 resembles a stadium with the lights down before a performance, twinkling only with camera flashes from the crowd. Unlike flashbulbs, though, these stars are no fleeting phenomenon: they have been shining for many billions of years.

The Milky Way's disc is ringed by more than 150 globular clusters, Messier 107 among them. Each of these spherical groups contains hundreds of thousands of extremely old stars, making them some of the oldest objects in our galaxy. How they formed, and what part they played in the evolution of galaxies, is still somewhat unclear, which is why astronomers keep studying them.

By globular standards, this cluster is fairly loose. Set beside others like Messier 53 or Messier 54, its stars are packed less tightly, so its members stand out more individually, like separate fans in the stands.
explore: About 20 000 light-years from the Solar System, Messier 107 lies in Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. Pierre Méchain first noted it in 1782 and William Herschel recorded it independently a year later; much later, the Canadian astronomer Helen Sawyer Hogg added it to Messier's catalogue. The image covers about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from the Wide Field Camera of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars that would blur together through a small telescope.

alt: A loosely packed crowd of stars in the globular cluster Messier 107.

caption: The globular cluster IC 4499, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble captures IC 4499 here, a globular cluster: one of the large, ball-shaped groups of old stars circling a galaxy. It has long been thought that all the stars in one form at about the same time, a property that can be used to work out a cluster's age.

For heavier globulars, careful observations tell a different story: they appear to hold several populations of stars born at different times. Gravity is thought to be one reason. IC 4499 is a useful in-between case, with a mass between the simple low-mass clusters and the more complex massive ones. Astronomers found no sign of multiple generations in it, supporting the idea that less massive clusters generally host just one.

Hubble has also helped pin down the cluster's age. Observations from the 1990s suggested it was puzzlingly young compared with other Milky Way globulars, but newer Hubble data make it much more likely that IC 4499 is roughly as old as the others, at about 12 billion years.
explore: IC 4499 lies about 55,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Apus. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through visible and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars in a distant cluster.

alt: A globular cluster of old stars.

caption: The globular cluster Terzan 7, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Terzan 7, a globular cluster that takes its name from Agop Terzan, the French-Armenian astronomer who found it. It is a densely packed ball of stars bound by gravity, lying just over 75 000 light-years away on the far side of the Milky Way, and it is peculiar in several ways.

Evidence shows that Terzan 7 once belonged to the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, a mini-galaxy that is colliding with the far larger Milky Way and being absorbed by it. The cluster seems to have already been pulled away from its former home and become part of our galaxy.

Astronomers found that all of Terzan 7's stars formed at roughly the same moment, some eight billion years ago, which is unusually young for such a cluster. A single generation is also uncommon, since many globular clusters seem to have at least two. Explanations vary: clusters born in dwarf galaxies may differ in composition, Terzan 7 may have had enough material for only one batch of stars, or it may simply be too young to have formed another.

caption: The centre of the globular cluster Messier 22, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the crowded centre of the globular cluster Messier 22. Globular clusters are ball-shaped swarms of tightly packed stars left over from the early Universe, typically 12 to 13 billion years old, which is remarkably old given that the Universe itself is only 13.8 billion years old.

At just 10 000 light-years away, Messier 22 is one of the closest of the Milky Way's roughly 150 globular clusters. Abraham Ihle discovered it in 1665, one of the earliest globulars to be discovered. Little wonder: it ranks among the brightest seen from the northern hemisphere, lying in Sagittarius near the Galactic Bulge. Even so, dust and gas between us and the cluster dim its starlight.

Messier 22 has some unusual residents. Six planet-sized objects that do not orbit any star have been detected there, the cluster seems to host two black holes, and it is among just three clusters known to hold a planetary nebula, a short-lived shell of gas thrown off by a dying star.
explore: The cluster is about 70 light-years across and covers a patch of sky as large as the full Moon. The image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.

caption: The young open cluster NGC 2367, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Colourful stars and gas spread across this rich view from the Wide Field Imager at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. The subject is NGC 2367, a young open cluster: an infant grouping of stars.

Curiously, this youthful cluster sits in the middle of a vast, much older structure out on the edges of the Milky Way. An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust, and a young one like this can still be surrounded by some of that gas.

The contrast is striking: a stellar infant set within something ancient. Young clusters are useful for studying how stars begin their lives, while their setting can hint at the longer history of the region around them.
explore: The picture was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, combining U, B, V and I filters with one that isolates the glow of hydrogen. NGC 2367 lies in the direction of the constellation Canis Major.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines U, B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, from the ultraviolet end of the spectrum into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.

caption: The open star cluster Messier 47, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A sprinkling of brilliant blue stars dominates this image of the star cluster Messier 47, with a few contrasting red giant stars among them. The picture was taken with the Wide Field Imager camera at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

Messier 47 is a young open cluster, a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. A star's colour reveals its surface temperature: the blue stars here are hot, while red giants are cooler stars that have swollen in size late in their lives.

Because all the stars in a cluster share roughly the same age, the mix of colours carries information. The most massive stars evolve fastest, so they are the first to become red giants, while less massive stars stay in their longer, steadier phase for much longer.
explore: The Wide Field Imager is mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. This colour picture was built from exposures through B, V and R filters, all in visible light. Messier 47 lies in the direction of the constellation Puppis.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The blue and red star colours reflect real temperature differences, but long exposures reveal far more stars than the eye could see.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 28, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In bright, sharp detail, Hubble reveals Messier 28, a globular cluster lying in Sagittarius, the Archer. It lies about 18 000 light-years from Earth.

When Charles Messier added it to his list in 1764, he described it as a '[round] nebula containing no star'. That was not as strange as it sounds. Until the early twentieth century, 'nebula' meant any hazy, poorly defined light in the sky, and all 110 objects Messier identified were gathered under the title Catalogue of Nebulae and Star Clusters. Star clusters and even supernova remnants were lumped together as nebulae.

Messier's mistake is understandable. From Earth, even through binoculars, the cluster appears only as a very faint smudge, because the atmosphere's distorting effects blur it, and larger telescopes are needed to pick out single stars. From space, Hubble shows it clearly as the star cluster it really is.
explore: Today, a nebula means a vast, often glowing cloud of interstellar dust and ionised gas. This image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 across a range of visible and near-infrared filters, including one that isolates glowing hydrogen.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from violet light through visible and hydrogen-alpha to the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars Messier 28 is only a very faint smudge; from above the atmosphere Hubble resolves its individual stars.

caption: The star cluster NGC 6193 and the nebula NGC 6188, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: The young open cluster NGC 6193 sits at the centre of this view from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory, with the emission nebula NGC 6188 to its right. Both belong to Ara OB1, a stellar association, and the picture shows one section of it.

An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that glows because it is energised by radiation. Here the ionising radiation comes from the brightest stars nearby, which strip electrons from the gas atoms; when the atoms recapture them, the gas gives off light.

A stellar association is a loose, widely spread group of stars that share a common origin. Young clusters like NGC 6193 and the glowing clouds beside them show star formation in progress, with newborn stars already lighting up the gas around them.
explore: The image was taken with OmegaCAM, the camera on the VLT Survey Telescope, using B, g, r and hydrogen-alpha filters. The region lies in the direction of the constellation Ara, the Altar.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope combines B, g, r and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures and a hydrogen-alpha filter bring out glowing gas far too faint for the eye to see like this.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Yellow squares mark some of the stars in this ESO image of NGC 6397, a nearby globular cluster about 7,200 light-years away in the southern constellation Ara. The highlighted stars were targets for detailed study with the FLAMES-UVES instrument.

NGC 6397 is described as metal-poor, meaning its stars contain relatively little of the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, which astronomers call metals. Stars poor in these elements generally formed early, before later generations of stars had enriched the gas of their galaxy.

Some of the brighter stars show spikes. These are not real features: they are caused by overexposure, when too much light floods the camera's detector, an effect known as CCD bleeding. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical group of old stars bound together by gravity.
explore: The picture is a composite of B, V and I exposures from La Silla's Wide Field Imager, made for the Pilot Stellar Survey and prepared by the ESO Imaging Survey team.

understand.summary: This composite comes from the Wide Field Imager, using B and V filters in visible light and an I filter in the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The yellow squares and the spikes on bright stars are added markings and camera artefacts, not things the eye would see in the sky.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 72, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Scattered stars fill this Hubble image of Messier 72, looking rather like a city seen from an aeroplane window at night, with small glints from suburban homes dotting the outskirts of a bright centre. In reality it is a globular cluster: an ancient ball of old stars that crowd together much more tightly toward the middle, like buildings at a city's heart.

Besides its own huge numbers of stars, the picture also catches many far more distant galaxies, visible between and around the cluster's stars. They are separate systems lying far beyond our galaxy, glimpsed through the gaps.

Pierre Méchain, a French astronomer, found the cluster in August 1780, yet it is named after his colleague Charles Messier, who logged it as the 72nd entry in his catalogue of comet-like objects only two months afterwards. Its home is Aquarius, the Water Bearer, some 50 000 light-years away.
explore: This was the first image in ESA/Hubble's weekly Picture of the Week series. It was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel through yellow and near-infrared filters, with exposures of about ten minutes each, and covers about 3.4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using yellow (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the distant background galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 7006, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 7006, a compact and distant globular cluster in Delphinus, the Dolphin, among the tiniest of the constellations. Because it is modest in size, very far away and relatively faint, amateur astronomers often overlook it, yet Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys renders it bright and clear.

NGC 7006 lies in the outskirts of the Milky Way, about 135 000 light-years away, or five times as far as the Sun is from the galactic centre. It belongs to the galactic halo, a roughly spherical zone of dark matter, gas and thinly spread star clusters. Its highly eccentric orbit hints that it may have been born on its own, inside a small outside galaxy that the Milky Way then captured.

Distant as it is, the cluster is far nearer than the numerous faint background galaxies in the frame. Each of those faint smudges probably has its own family of globular clusters like NGC 7006, too faint for even Hubble to see.
explore: Remote clusters like this one offer important clues to how stars formed and gathered in the Milky Way's halo. The image combines visible and near-infrared light and covers a field a little over 3 by 3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and this cluster is too faint and small for most amateur telescopes to show in such detail.

caption: The super star cluster Westerlund 1 and the red supergiant W26, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Green features in this image from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory are clouds of glowing hydrogen gas around W26, a red supergiant in the super star cluster Westerlund 1. W26 is possibly the biggest star known, and finding such clouds around it was a surprise.

Westerlund 1 shines exceptionally brightly from about 16 000 light-years away, in Ara, the Altar, a southern constellation. It holds hundreds of very massive, brilliant stars, none more than a few million years old, but gas and dust block most of its visible light from reaching us. Such glowing clouds are rare around massive stars, and this is the first ionised nebula ever found around a red supergiant.

W26 is not hot enough to light the gas itself. The team speculates that the energy comes either from other hot blue stars in the cluster or from a fainter but much hotter companion. W26 will eventually explode as a supernova, and studying its nebula should help show how such stars lose mass before their explosive end.
explore: The picture belongs to VPHAS+, a public survey that uses the VST to map much of the Milky Way in detail, hunting for new objects, among them young stars and planetary nebulae. The nebula around W26 closely resembles the one around SN1987A, the closest supernova seen from Earth since 1604.

understand.summary: This image from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope combines G, R, I and hydrogen-alpha filters. The glowing hydrogen around W26 is shown in green; the other colour assignments aren't published.
understand.eye: Dust blocks most of this cluster's visible light, and the hydrogen glow appears green here only because that colour was chosen to display it.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 54, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Messier 54, a dense, faint group of stars that could pass for just another globular cluster. In fact it was the first globular cluster found outside our galaxy. Charles Messier discovered it in 1778, and it belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy, a satellite of the Milky Way.

Messier had no idea of its significance. Only in 1994, more than two centuries later, did astronomers realise that it belongs to the small galaxy rather than our own. Current estimates put the Sagittarius dwarf, and so the cluster, almost 90 000 light-years away, which puts it over three times farther from the galactic centre than the Solar System.

There is an irony here. Although Messier 54 lies outside the Milky Way today, it will become part of it. The Milky Way's powerful gravity is gradually swallowing the Sagittarius dwarf, and in time the two will merge into one larger galaxy.
explore: The picture combines images from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel, with total exposures of 3460 and 3560 seconds, and covers about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes. A dwarf elliptical galaxy is a small, faint galaxy with a smooth, rounded shape.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a yellow-orange filter (F606W) is shown in blue and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the colours are reassigned rather than natural.

caption: The core of the globular cluster NGC 6362, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble takes a deep look into the core of the globular cluster NGC 6362, where a high concentration of stars shines in a range of different colours. Globular clusters are spherical collections of old stars, tightly bound by gravity; at around 10 billion years old, their stars are much older than the Sun.

More than 150 are known in the Milky Way, and more have been found in other galaxies. They rank among the oldest things in the Universe we can study directly, living fossils of the early cosmos. For years they were seen as ideal laboratories for testing the standard theory of stellar evolution, which suggests that most stars in a globular cluster should be of similar age.

High-precision measurements, mainly with Hubble, have led some to question that picture. Certain stars, called blue stragglers, look younger and bluer than their companions, and NGC 6362 contains many of them. Because they usually sit in crowded cores, the likeliest explanation is stellar collisions or material passing between stars in binary pairs, which heats a star and makes it look younger.
explore: About 25 000 light-years away, NGC 6362 is found in Ara, the Altar, and the British astronomer James Dunlop was the first to observe it. The image combines ultraviolet, visible and infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: This image combines ultraviolet light from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 with red and near-infrared light from its Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates the crowded stars of the core.
