caption: The star cluster NGC 3572 and its surroundings, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Clouds of gas and dust around the young star cluster NGC 3572 have been carved into playful bubbles and arcs, along with curious shapes called elephant trunks, in this image from ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. The shaping is done by stellar winds flowing from the cluster's bright stars.

NGC 3572 is a gathering of young stars, and ESO describes this as the best image of it so far, made with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager. Elephant trunks are dense columns of gas and dust that resist erosion by the winds and radiation of nearby stars, leaving pillar-like shapes behind.

The cluster's brightest members outweigh the Sun, and their brief lives will finish in supernova explosions. Massive stars burn through their fuel much faster than lower-mass ones, which is why the most luminous members of a young cluster are also the shortest-lived.
explore: The picture combines two visible-light filters, B and V, with a hydrogen-alpha filter that isolates the glow of hydrogen gas in the surrounding clouds. NGC 3572 lies in the direction of the constellation Carina.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B and V filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures and a hydrogen-alpha filter reveal faint glowing gas that the eye could not see.

caption: The spiral structure around the red giant R Sculptoris, imaged by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)
story: An outer circular ring encloses a clear spiral pattern in this view of the gas and dust surrounding R Sculptoris, an old star. The picture is a slice through observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA): the ring is a shell around the star, and the spiral lies in the material inside it.

The spiral was unexpected and had never been seen before. A likely cause is an unseen companion star in orbit around R Sculptoris, which could wind the material around the old star into a spiral as it circles.

R Sculptoris is classed as a red giant, an ageing star that has swollen up and sheds material into space. ALMA works at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, picking up the faint glow of cool gas and dust that visible-light telescopes cannot easily see. Because this is a slice through the data rather than a conventional picture, it shows structure in a way no ordinary photograph could.
explore: R Sculptoris lies about 1500 light-years away and is also a variable star, one whose brightness changes over time. ALMA observed it in its Band 7, at a wavelength of about 870 micrometres.

understand.summary: ALMA observed this star at submillimetre wavelengths (Band 7, 870 μm). This is a data visualisation, and its colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Submillimetre light is invisible to the eye, and this image is a slice through the data rather than a view of the sky as it would look.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 1783 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 1783's symmetry and the crowding of its stars toward the centre stand out plainly in this image from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Both are typical features of globular clusters, tightly packed, self-gravitating star groups that circle galaxies like satellites.

Among the largest globulars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy that orbits our own, NGC 1783 lies nearly 160 000 light-years from Earth. John Herschel first observed it in 1835. It weighs in at around 170 000 Suns.

From the colours and brightnesses of its individual stars, astronomers estimate that NGC 1783 has existed for less than one and a half billion years, which is very young for a globular. It is thought to have had at least two bursts of star formation, 50 to 100 million years apart. The idea is that supernovae from the first massive stars blew away the leftover gas, which gentler, longer-lived stars later replenished before a second round began.
explore: This ebb and flow can repeat a few times, until the remaining gas is thought to be too little to form new stars. The cluster lies in the southern constellation Dorado, and Judy Schmidt entered a version of this image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.
